title: Second Temple of Hera, Paestum
creator: greek-master-builders
note: One of the best-preserved Doric temples anywhere, in a Greek colony in southern Italy.
description: Paestum, the Greek colony of Poseidonia south of Naples, preserves three Doric temples. The largest and best preserved, built around 460 BC and traditionally called the Temple of Neptune, is now usually identified as a second temple of Hera, though its dedication is uncertain. It has six by fourteen massive fluted columns with a pronounced swelling, or entasis, and its interior still carries two tiers of smaller columns that supported the roof. Built of local travertine, once stuccoed and painted, it shows the mature Doric order shortly before the Parthenon. The site was abandoned in the Middle Ages and rediscovered in the eighteenth century, when engravings by Piranesi and visits by architects such as Soufflot made its heavy, primitive-seeming columns a powerful influence on the Greek Revival.
image_caption: Second Temple of Hera, Paestum, Paestum, Campania, Italy

title: Parthenon
creator: ictinus
note: The temple of Athena on the Acropolis, the summit of the Doric order and of classical Greek architecture.
description: The Parthenon was built under Pericles to house Phidias's gold and ivory statue of Athena Parthenos, replacing an earlier temple destroyed by the Persians in 480 BC. Ictinus and Callicrates designed it, and Phidias oversaw its sculpture: the pediments, ninety-two metopes and a continuous Ionic frieze, probably showing the Panathenaic procession. The temple has eight by seventeen Doric columns in Pentelic marble, and almost nothing in it is straight: the platform curves upward, the columns lean slightly inward and swell, and the corner columns are thicker, refinements intended to correct optical illusions and give the building life. Over the centuries it served as a church, a mosque and a gunpowder store; a Venetian shell blew up its centre in 1687, and in the early nineteenth century Lord Elgin removed much of the sculpture to London, where its return remains a matter of dispute. Restoration has been under way since the 1970s.
image_caption: Parthenon, Acropolis, Athens, Greece

title: Temple of Athena Nike
creator: callicrates
note: A small, elegant Ionic temple on the bastion at the entrance to the Acropolis.
description: The temple of Athena Nike, Athena as goddess of victory, stands on a projecting bastion beside the Propylaea, the gateway to the Acropolis. A decree of the mid-fifth century entrusted its design to Callicrates, but it was built only in the 420s, during the Peloponnesian War. It is an amphiprostyle temple, with four slender Ionic columns at front and back and none along the sides, and a sculpted frieze showing gods and battles, including Greeks fighting Persians. A parapet around the bastion carried famous reliefs of winged Victories, among them one adjusting her sandal, now in the Acropolis Museum. The Ottomans dismantled the temple in 1686 to build a gun battery; it was reassembled from its original blocks in the 1830s and again in recent decades.
image_file: Temple of Athena Nikè from Propylaea, Acropolis, Athens, Greece.jpg
image_caption: Temple of Athena Nike, Acropolis, Athens, Greece

title: Erechtheion
creator: greek-master-builders
note: An irregular Ionic temple of several cults, famous for its porch of maidens, the Caryatids.
description: The Erechtheion, on the north side of the Acropolis, housed the ancient olive-wood statue of Athena Polias and shrines to Poseidon, the legendary king Erechtheus and other cults on a site holding sacred marks of the contest between Athena and Poseidon. Its unknown architect, sometimes thought to be Mnesicles, resolved a sloping site and multiple functions in an asymmetrical building with porches on three sides and floors at different levels. The finely carved Ionic columns and the south porch, where six maidens, the Caryatids, serve as columns, made it the model for the Ionic order in later centuries. Building accounts inscribed in stone record the wages of the citizens, foreigners and slaves who worked on it. One Caryatid is in the British Museum; the others are in the Acropolis Museum and copies stand in their place.
image_caption: Erechtheion, Acropolis, Athens, Greece

title: Propylaea of the Acropolis
creator: greek-master-builders
note: Mnesicles's monumental entrance to the Acropolis, combining Doric and Ionic orders.
description: The Propylaea, designed according to Plutarch by the architect Mnesicles, is the grand marble gateway at the west end of the Acropolis, begun as soon as the Parthenon was complete. Facing the ascending visitor are two Doric porches like temple fronts, and the central passage through which processions climbed is lined with Ionic columns, an early combination of the two orders in one building. A wing to the north, the Pinakotheke, displayed paintings. The building was never finished: work stopped with the Peloponnesian War, and lifting bosses still project from some blocks. Later used as a palace and a gunpowder store, it inspired monumental gateways from the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin to the Propyläen in Munich.
image_file: East Facade of the Propylaea on July 23, 2019.jpg
image_caption: Propylaea of the Acropolis, Acropolis, Athens, Greece

title: Theatre of Epidaurus
creator: greek-master-builders
note: The best-preserved Greek theatre, renowned for its proportions and acoustics.
description: The theatre in the sanctuary of Asclepius at Epidaurus, a healing centre that drew pilgrims from across Greece, was built in the late fourth century BC and extended in the second. Pausanias attributed it to Polykleitos the Younger, an attribution modern scholars treat with caution. Its limestone seats, for around 13,000 spectators, rise in a slightly more than semicircular bowl around a full circular orchestra, set into a natural hillside. The theatre is famous for its acoustics, which carry even a whisper from the orchestra to the upper rows, an effect researchers have linked to the way the rows of seats filter low-frequency noise. Buried for centuries and excavated from 1881, it is again used for performances of ancient drama each summer.

title: De architectura (Ten Books on Architecture)
creator: vitruvius
location: Rome; earliest manuscripts c. 800, first printed c. 1486
note: The only complete architectural treatise to survive from antiquity, foundation of Western architectural theory.
description: Vitruvius dedicated his ten books on architecture to Augustus. They cover the education of the architect, building materials, temples and the orders, public buildings such as theatres and baths, private houses, wall painting and stucco, water and aqueducts, astronomy and sundials, and machines for war and peace. The work defines architecture by the triad of firmness, commodity and delight, and relates the proportions of buildings to the well-built human body. It survived in medieval manuscripts, was studied by humanists such as Poggio Bracciolini and Alberti, and was first printed in Rome around 1486. Illustrated editions, such as Fra Giocondo's of 1511 and Daniele Barbaro's with drawings by Palladio, made it the bible of Renaissance and Neoclassical architects, even though its diagrams were lost and its meaning often obscure.
image_caption: De architectura, early printed edition

title: Maison Carrée
creator: roman-builders
note: One of the best-preserved Roman temples, the model for Jefferson's Virginia State Capitol.
description: The Maison Carrée ('square house') at Nîmes, in the Roman province of Gallia Narbonensis, was built under Augustus and rededicated to his grandsons and adopted heirs Gaius and Lucius Caesar. It is a classic Roman temple: raised on a high podium, approached by a frontal stair, with a deep porch of six Corinthian columns and half-columns engaged in the walls of the cella along the sides and back. Its survival almost intact is due to continuous use as a meeting hall, a stable, a church and a museum. Thomas Jefferson, who saw it in 1787 and said he gazed at it for hours, used it as the model for the Virginia State Capitol, and it inspired the Madeleine in Paris. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.
image_caption: Maison Carrée, Nîmes, France

title: Pont du Gard
creator: roman-builders
note: The tallest surviving Roman aqueduct bridge, carrying water to Nîmes across the Gardon river.
description: The Pont du Gard carried the aqueduct that brought water about fifty kilometres from springs near Uzès to the Roman city of Nemausus (Nîmes). It is usually dated to the mid-first century AD. Three tiers of arches, built of huge limestone blocks laid without mortar, rise nearly fifty metres above the Gardon river, and the water channel on top descends by only a few centimetres across the bridge, part of a gradient for the whole aqueduct of about twenty-five centimetres per kilometre. Projecting stones and ridges left in the masonry supported scaffolding. The aqueduct fell out of use by the sixth century, but the bridge survived because it served as a road crossing, and it became a celebrated stop on the Grand Tour. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_caption: Pont du Gard, Vers-Pont-du-Gard, near Nîmes, France

title: Colosseum (Flavian Amphitheatre)
creator: roman-builders
note: The largest amphitheatre of the Roman world, built for gladiatorial games and spectacles.
description: The emperor Vespasian began the Flavian Amphitheatre around AD 70 on the site of the lake of Nero's Golden House, and his son Titus inaugurated it in 80 with a hundred days of games; Domitian completed it. An ellipse about 189 by 156 metres, it held perhaps 50,000 spectators, seated by rank and admitted through eighty numbered entrances. Its outer wall stacks three storeys of arches framed by Tuscan, Ionic and Corinthian half-columns beneath an attic of Corinthian pilasters, a sequence that became a rule for Renaissance architects. Under the arena, the hypogeum held animals, gladiators and lifts. After the games ended in the sixth century it served as housing, fortress and quarry; earthquakes and stone robbing reduced it to its present state. It remains the symbol of Rome.
image_caption: Colosseum (Flavian Amphitheatre), Rome, Italy

title: Trajan's Column
creator: apollodorus
note: A marble column wound with a spiral relief of Trajan's Dacian Wars, the centrepiece of his forum.
description: Trajan's Column stood in a courtyard between the libraries of Trajan's Forum, a complex usually credited to Apollodorus of Damascus, and was dedicated in 113. About thirty metres tall, it is built from nineteen drums of Carrara marble, hollowed out to contain a spiral staircase lit by small windows. A continuous relief band some 200 metres long spirals twenty-three times around the shaft, depicting Trajan's two campaigns against the Dacians with over 2,500 figures: marching, building, fighting and negotiating. The emperor's ashes were placed in its base, and a statue of Trajan crowned it until it was replaced in 1587 by Saint Peter. Its relief is a key source for the Roman army, and the column inspired imitations from the column of Marcus Aurelius to the Vendôme Column in Paris.
image_caption: Trajan's Column, Trajan's Forum, Rome, Italy

title: Pantheon
creator: roman-builders
note: The domed temple of all the gods, the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
description: The Pantheon was rebuilt under Hadrian on the site of a temple built by Marcus Agrippa, whose name is still inscribed on the portico; its architect is unknown, though Apollodorus of Damascus has sometimes been suggested. A traditional temple porch of sixteen granite Corinthian columns leads into a vast rotunda whose height and diameter are equal, about 43 metres, so that a sphere would fit within it. The concrete of the coffered dome grows lighter toward the top, with pumice in the aggregate, and the dome is open at the crown in an oculus nearly nine metres across, the only source of light. Consecrated as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres in 609, it has been in use ever since and contains the tombs of Raphael and the kings of Italy. It is the most influential surviving building of antiquity, the ancestor of domed buildings from Florence to Washington.
image_caption: Pantheon, Rome, Italy

title: Hadrian's Villa
creator: roman-builders
note: The emperor Hadrian's vast country retreat, a laboratory of Roman architectural forms.
description: Hadrian, the most architecturally minded of Roman emperors and possibly involved in the design himself, built a retreat below the hills of Tivoli covering more than a hundred hectares. It contains over thirty buildings: palaces, baths, libraries, theatres, guest quarters and gardens, laid out on varying axes. The so-called Maritime Theatre is a round island villa within a moat, and the Canopus is a long pool framed by colonnades and statues, said to recall places Hadrian had visited in Egypt. Its domes and vaults on curved and lobed plans show Roman concrete architecture at its most inventive. Plundered for marble and sculpture after antiquity, it was excavated from the Renaissance onward and studied by Piranesi and later architects. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_caption: Hadrian's Villa, Tivoli, near Rome, Italy

title: Baths of Caracalla
creator: roman-builders
note: A colossal imperial bath complex whose vaulted halls inspired later architects.
description: The Baths of Caracalla, built under the emperors Septimius Severus and Caracalla, were among the largest public baths of Rome, used by several thousand people at a time. A central bathing block, with a cold-water hall, a warm room and a circular hot room, the caldarium, under a great dome, stood within a precinct of gardens, libraries and exercise areas. Behind the scenes, furnaces, aqueduct-fed cisterns and underground passages for slaves heated and supplied the complex. The baths functioned until the Gothic siege of 537 cut the aqueducts. Their immense brick-faced concrete ruins influenced Renaissance and modern architects; the waiting hall of New York's demolished Pennsylvania Station was modelled on them. Operas are performed in the ruins in summer.
image_caption: Baths of Caracalla, Rome, Italy

title: Santa Sabina
creator: byzantine-builders
note: The best-preserved early Christian basilica in Rome, with its original cypress-wood doors.
description: Santa Sabina was built by Peter of Illyria, a priest, in the time of Pope Celestine I, as recorded in a mosaic inscription over the entrance. It is the classic early Christian basilica: a tall nave lined with twenty-four reused fluted Corinthian columns carrying arcades, high clerestory windows, aisles, and an apse at the end, with an emphasis on light and calm proportion. Much of its marble inlay has been lost, but its carved cypress doors, with panels of biblical scenes, include one of the earliest surviving depictions of the crucifixion. Given to Saint Dominic in 1222, it is still the headquarters of the Dominican order. Restorations in the early twentieth century removed later alterations to recover its original appearance.
image_caption: Santa Sabina, Aventine Hill, Rome, Italy

title: Basilica of San Vitale
creator: byzantine-builders
note: An octagonal Byzantine church famous for its mosaics of Justinian and Theodora.
description: San Vitale was begun under Bishop Ecclesius when Ravenna was ruled by the Ostrogoths, funded by the banker Julianus Argentarius, and consecrated in 547 after the city had been retaken by Justinian's Byzantine Empire. Its plan is an octagon whose central domed space is surrounded by an ambulatory and gallery, opening through curved columned niches so that space seems to flow outward. The plain brick exterior contrasts with an interior of marble and mosaic, above all the apse panels in which the emperor Justinian and empress Theodora, with their courts, bring offerings to the altar. San Vitale was a model for Charlemagne's chapel at Aachen. With other Ravenna monuments it forms a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_caption: Basilica of San Vitale, Ravenna, Italy

title: Hagia Sophia
creator: anthemius-isidore
note: Justinian's great church of Holy Wisdom, whose dome was the wonder of the medieval world.
description: After the Nika riots burned the previous church in 532, the emperor Justinian had Hagia Sophia, the church of Holy Wisdom, rebuilt in less than six years under the mathematicians Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus. They combined a basilica with a centralised plan: a dome about 31 metres across rises on four pendentives, curved triangles that turn a square into a circle, and is extended east and west by half-domes so that the nave forms one enormous space. A ring of forty windows at the base makes the dome seem to float on light, and the interior was clad in coloured marble and gold mosaic. The first dome fell in 558 and was rebuilt higher. For nearly a thousand years the cathedral of Constantinople, it became a mosque after the Ottoman conquest in 1453, with minarets added, a museum in 1934 and a mosque again in 2020. It inspired Ottoman architects such as Sinan.
image_caption: Hagia Sophia, Istanbul, Turkey

title: St Mark's Basilica
creator: byzantine-builders
note: Venice's five-domed church of the Doge, glittering with gold mosaic.
description: St Mark's was built as the chapel of the Doge of Venice to house the relics of Saint Mark, stolen from Alexandria in 828. The present church, begun in 1063 and consecrated in 1094, follows the plan of the lost Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople: a Greek cross with a dome over the crossing and each arm. Over the following centuries the Venetians covered it with more than 8,000 square metres of gold-ground mosaic, raised taller outer domes, and encrusted the façade with marble, sculptures and spoils, including the bronze horses taken from Constantinople in the Fourth Crusade of 1204. Its mixture of Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic and Islamic elements reflects Venice's position between East and West. It became the cathedral of Venice in 1807.
image_file: Venezia Basilica di San Marco Fassade 2.jpg
image_caption: St Mark's Basilica, Venice, Italy

title: Palatine Chapel, Aachen
creator: odo-of-metz
note: Charlemagne's octagonal chapel, the oldest part of Aachen Cathedral and a founding monument of medieval architecture.
description: Charlemagne built his palace at Aachen in the 790s, and its chapel, consecrated by Pope Leo III according to tradition in 805, survives as the core of Aachen Cathedral. Attributed to Odo of Metz, it is an octagon of stone covered by a domed vault, surrounded by a sixteen-sided ambulatory and a gallery where the emperor's throne still stands. The design draws on San Vitale in Ravenna but is heavier and more geometric, and Charlemagne brought ancient columns and marble from Rome and Ravenna. Charlemagne was buried there in 814, and for six centuries German kings were crowned on his throne. A Gothic glass choir was added in the fourteenth century. The cathedral was among the first sites inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1978.
image_caption: Palatine Chapel, Aachen, Aachen, Germany

title: Speyer Cathedral
creator: romanesque-builders
note: The burial church of the Salian emperors, one of the largest Romanesque buildings in Europe.
description: The emperor Conrad II began the cathedral at Speyer around 1030 as a dynastic burial church, and his grandson Henry IV rebuilt it on an even grander scale from about 1080, vaulting the nave in stone. With its long nave, towers at each end and domes over the crossing and westwork, it was meant to rival the great churches of antiquity and to proclaim imperial power at the height of the Investiture Contest with the papacy. The nave's groin vaults, among the largest of their time, rest on alternating piers with half-columns rising the full height of the walls. Eight emperors and kings are buried in its crypt. Damaged by fire in 1689, it was rebuilt and restored in the eighteenth to twentieth centuries and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_caption: Speyer Cathedral, Speyer, Germany

title: Basilica of Saint-Sernin
creator: romanesque-builders
note: The largest surviving Romanesque church in Europe, on the pilgrimage road to Santiago.
description: Saint-Sernin was built over the tomb of Saint Saturninus, first bishop of Toulouse, to receive pilgrims on the way to Santiago de Compostela. Its altar was consecrated in 1096. It is a model pilgrimage church: a long barrel-vaulted nave with double aisles, a transept with aisles, and an ambulatory with radiating chapels that allowed crowds to circulate past relics without disturbing services. The building is mostly in the red brick of Toulouse with stone details, and its octagonal crossing tower rises in tiers. Sculpture of the late eleventh century, in the Porte Miègeville and the marble reliefs in the ambulatory, is among the earliest monumental Romanesque carving. Viollet-le-Duc's nineteenth-century restoration was partly reversed in the 1990s.
image_file: Basilique Saint-Sernin de Toulouse - exposition ouest-1-.jpg
image_caption: Basilica of Saint-Sernin, Toulouse, France

title: Durham Cathedral
creator: romanesque-builders
note: A massive Norman cathedral with some of the earliest rib vaults in Europe.
description: Durham Cathedral was begun in 1093 by Bishop William of St Calais, one of the Norman prelates installed after the Conquest, to house the shrine of Saint Cuthbert and the remains of Bede. Set high above a loop of the River Wear beside the castle, it was built largely in forty years. Its nave alternates huge compound piers with cylindrical columns carved with chevrons, spirals and flutes, and its stone ribbed vaults, with pointed transverse arches in the nave, are among the earliest in Europe, anticipating the structural system of Gothic. The Galilee Chapel and the Chapel of the Nine Altars were added in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Together with the castle it forms a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is often called the finest Norman building in England.
image_caption: Durham Cathedral, Durham, England

title: Pisa Cathedral and Leaning Tower
creator: romanesque-builders
note: Pisa's marble cathedral complex, with its famously leaning bell tower.
description: Pisa, then a rich maritime republic, began its cathedral in 1063, paid for with spoils from a raid on Palermo. Its architect Buscheto is buried in the façade. Built of white and grey marble, it combines a basilica with a dome over the crossing, and its façade of stacked open arcades became the hallmark of Pisan Romanesque. The circular baptistery was begun in 1152 and the bell tower in 1173; the tower began to lean during construction because of soft ground, and its builders, resuming work after long pauses, curved the upper storeys to compensate. It was completed in 1372 and by the late twentieth century leaned about 5.5 degrees; engineering work in 1990–2001 reduced the tilt and stabilised it. With the cemetery, the Camposanto, the ensemble forms the Piazza dei Miracoli, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_file: View of the Cathedral facade from the Baptistry (Pisa).jpg
image_caption: Pisa Cathedral and Leaning Tower, Piazza dei Miracoli, Pisa, Italy

title: Basilica of Saint-Denis
creator: abbot-suger
note: The abbey church where Suger's new choir of 1140–44 launched the Gothic style.
description: The royal abbey of Saint-Denis held the relics of the patron saint of France and the tombs of its kings. Abbot Suger rebuilt the west end around 1135–40 with a façade of three portals and twin towers and a rose window, and then a new choir, consecrated in 1144 before the king and many bishops. In the choir, an anonymous master combined pointed arches, rib vaults and slender columns to create a double ambulatory with radiating chapels whose walls are almost entirely stained glass, so that the whole east end shines with what Suger called uninterrupted light. The nave and transept were rebuilt in the Rayonnant style from 1231. The tombs were desecrated during the Revolution and later restored. Saint-Denis became a cathedral in 1966.
image_caption: Basilica of Saint-Denis, Saint-Denis, near Paris, France

title: Chartres Cathedral
creator: chartres-master-builders
note: The most complete High Gothic cathedral, with its original stained glass and sculpture largely intact.
description: Chartres was a great centre of devotion to the Virgin, whose tunic was its chief relic. After a fire in 1194 destroyed most of the earlier church, the cathedral was rebuilt in about twenty-five years around the surviving west façade with its twelfth-century Royal Portal. The new building set the pattern of High Gothic: a nave elevation of arcade, narrow triforium and a clerestory as tall as the arcade, quadripartite vaults and flying buttresses. Some 170 windows preserve most of their original thirteenth-century glass, including the Notre-Dame de la Belle Verrière and three great roses, and thousands of sculpted figures fill the transept portals. The two west spires differ: the south is Romanesque, the north flamboyant Gothic of the early sixteenth century. A UNESCO World Heritage Site, it was cleaned and restored in the 2000s and 2010s.
image_caption: Chartres Cathedral, Chartres, France

title: Notre-Dame de Paris
creator: notre-dame-master-builders
location: Île de la Cité, Paris, France
note: The cathedral of Paris, a pioneer of Gothic design and a symbol of France.
description: Bishop Maurice de Sully began Notre-Dame in 1163, and the choir, nave and west façade were built over the next eighty years. The early design, with galleries over the aisles and six-part vaults, was enlarged in the thirteenth century with taller clerestory windows, flying buttresses among the earliest of their kind, and the great rose windows of the transepts by Jean de Chelles and Pierre de Montreuil. The west front, with its three sculpted portals, gallery of kings and twin towers, is a model of balance. Damaged in the Revolution and neglected, the cathedral was made famous anew by Victor Hugo's novel of 1831 and restored by Lassus and Viollet-le-Duc, who added the spire. On 15 April 2019 a fire destroyed the roof and spire; after five years of reconstruction, the cathedral reopened in December 2024.
image_caption: Notre-Dame de Paris, Île de la Cité, Paris, France

title: Sainte-Chapelle
creator: pierre-de-montreuil
location: Île de la Cité, Paris, France
note: Louis IX's reliquary chapel, a cage of stained glass and the masterpiece of the Rayonnant style.
description: King Louis IX built the Sainte-Chapelle within the royal palace in Paris to house the Crown of Thorns and other Passion relics he had bought from the Latin emperor of Constantinople. It was consecrated in 1248. A lower chapel served the palace staff; the upper chapel, for the king, is a single vessel in which the walls are reduced to slender piers between fifteen windows about fifteen metres tall, showing over a thousand scenes from the Bible culminating in the story of the relics. Iron bars and chains concealed in the masonry help stabilise the structure. The chapel is traditionally, but not certainly, attributed to Pierre de Montreuil. The relics were dispersed in the Revolution, and the chapel was extensively restored in the nineteenth century; about two thirds of the glass is original.
image_caption: Sainte-Chapelle, the upper chapel with its stained glass

title: Amiens Cathedral
creator: gothic-master-builders
note: The largest Gothic cathedral in France, a summit of High Gothic design by Robert de Luzarches.
description: Amiens Cathedral was begun in 1220 to house the relic of the head of John the Baptist. A labyrinth in the nave floor names its designer, Robert de Luzarches, and his successors Thomas and Renaud de Cormont. Built rapidly to a unified design, it has an interior volume of about 200,000 cubic metres and a nave vault 42 metres high. Its tall arcade, glazed triforium in the choir and huge clerestory give an effect of soaring lightness. The west front's three portals, with the figure of Christ known as the Beau Dieu, form one of the great sculptural programmes of the Middle Ages, and laser cleaning revealed traces of its original paint. John Ruskin wrote a guide to it, The Bible of Amiens. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_caption: Amiens Cathedral, Amiens, France

title: Reims Cathedral
creator: gothic-master-builders
note: The coronation cathedral of the French kings, celebrated for its sculpture.
description: Reims Cathedral stands where Clovis, king of the Franks, was baptised around 500, and almost all French kings were crowned there. After a fire in 1210 the cathedral was rebuilt from 1211; a lost labyrinth named Jean d'Orbais, Jean le Loup, Gaucher de Reims and Bernard de Soissons as its masters. The building introduced bar tracery, in which windows are divided by thin stone bars, a decisive step for later Gothic. Its west front, with rose window and portals glazed rather than filled with sculpted tympana, carries some 2,300 statues, including the smiling angel. German shelling in the First World War set the cathedral on fire and badly damaged it, an event that became a symbol of wartime destruction; restoration, aided by the Rockefeller family, allowed reopening in 1938. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_file: Exterior view of the west facade of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Reims.jpg
image_caption: Reims Cathedral, Reims, France

title: Salisbury Cathedral
creator: gothic-master-builders
note: An Early English Gothic cathedral built to a single design, with the tallest spire in Britain.
description: In 1220 the bishop and canons left their windswept hilltop cathedral at Old Sarum and began a new one in the meadows below, and the main building was completed in only thirty-eight years, giving it unusual unity. It is the classic example of the Early English Gothic style: long and low, with double transepts, lancet windows, dark Purbeck marble shafts, and a vast walled close of lawns. The tower and spire, added around 1320, reach about 123 metres, the tallest in Britain, and their weight has visibly bent the crossing piers. The chapter house holds one of the four surviving original copies of Magna Carta of 1215. John Constable's paintings made the cathedral seen across the water meadows one of the best-known images of England.
image_caption: Salisbury Cathedral, Salisbury, England

title: Cologne Cathedral
creator: gothic-master-builders
note: A High Gothic cathedral begun in 1248 and completed only in 1880, with twin spires 157 metres tall.
description: Cologne Cathedral was begun in 1248 under Master Gerhard to house the relics of the Three Kings, brought from Milan in 1164. Its choir, modelled on Amiens and Sainte-Chapelle, was consecrated in 1322, but work stopped around 1473, leaving a medieval crane standing on the unfinished south tower for four centuries. The rediscovery of medieval drawings of the façade in the early nineteenth century and Romantic and nationalist enthusiasm led to completion between 1842 and 1880, with funding from the Prussian state and a public building society; it was briefly the tallest building in the world. It survived Allied bombing in the Second World War though hit many times. Its five-aisled nave, treasury and stained glass, including a window by Gerhard Richter of 2007, attract millions of visitors. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_file: Kölner Dom - Westfassade 2022 ohne Gerüst-0968 b.jpg
image_caption: Cologne Cathedral, Cologne, Germany

title: St Vitus Cathedral
creator: parler
note: The cathedral of Prague Castle, begun by Matthias of Arras and continued by Peter Parler.
description: When Prague became an archbishopric in 1344, the future Emperor Charles IV began a new cathedral within Prague Castle, first under Matthias of Arras, who built a French-style choir, and from 1356 under Peter Parler. Parler and his sons built the upper choir with its innovative net vault, the chapel of Saint Wenceslas lined with semi-precious stones and wall paintings, the Golden Gate with its mosaic of the Last Judgement, and the base of the great tower. The triforium contains busts of the royal family, archbishops and the architects themselves. The Hussite wars stopped work, and the nave and west front were completed only between 1873 and 1929 in a Gothic Revival style. It holds the tombs of Bohemian kings and the Bohemian crown jewels.
image_caption: St Vitus Cathedral, Prague Castle, Prague, Czech Republic

title: Florence Campanile
creator: giotto
note: The marble-clad bell tower of Florence Cathedral, begun by Giotto.
description: Giotto, appointed master of works of the cathedral in 1334, laid the foundations of the bell tower that year and built its lowest storey. After his death in 1337 Andrea Pisano continued it, adding the niches for statues, and Francesco Talenti completed it around 1359 with the tall windowed upper storeys, abandoning the spire Giotto may have planned. Some 85 metres tall, the square tower is clad in white Carrara, green Prato and pink Maremma marble in geometric panels matching the cathedral. Its lower storeys carry hexagonal and lozenge reliefs by Pisano, Luca della Robbia and others showing the creation of man, the arts and sciences, the planets and the sacraments, and its niches once held statues by Donatello, now in the cathedral museum. It is part of the historic centre of Florence, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_caption: Florence Campanile, Florence, Italy

title: Palazzo Vecchio
creator: arnolfo
note: The fortress-like town hall of republican Florence, with its tall off-centre tower.
description: The Palazzo dei Priori, later called the Palazzo Vecchio, was built from 1299 to house the government of the Florentine republic, the Signoria. Vasari attributed it to Arnolfo di Cambio, a plausible but undocumented attribution. It is a massive block of rusticated stone, crowned by projecting battlements on corbels and by a slender tower 94 metres tall, built over an older tower and set off-centre. The Medici, who became dukes, lived here in the sixteenth century and had Vasari remodel the interiors, including the vast Hall of the Five Hundred; Leonardo and Michelangelo had been commissioned to paint battle scenes for it, which were never completed. It remains Florence's town hall and a museum, and Michelangelo's David stood before it until 1873, where a copy now stands.
image_file: Piazza della signoria, palazzo vecchio, veduta 01.jpg
image_caption: Palazzo Vecchio, Piazza della Signoria, Florence, Italy

title: King's College Chapel
creator: gothic-master-builders
note: A late Gothic chapel famous for its fan vault, the largest in the world.
description: Henry VI founded King's College in 1441 and laid the foundation stone of its chapel in 1446, but the Wars of the Roses interrupted building, and it was completed under Henry VII and Henry VIII. The chapel is a single tall space, nearly 90 metres long, in the Perpendicular Gothic style, with walls almost entirely of glass framed by buttresses. The master mason John Wastell built its fan vault in 1508–15, a stone ceiling of cone-shaped fans with fine tracery, the largest of its kind. The windows, made mostly in the 1510s–40s by Flemish and English glaziers, form the most complete set of Renaissance-era glass in England, and Henry VIII's oak screen bears the initials of Anne Boleyn. The college choir's Christmas Eve Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols, broadcast since 1928, has made the interior famous worldwide.
image_caption: King's College Chapel, Cambridge, England

title: Basilica of Santa Croce
creator: arnolfo
note: The great Franciscan church of Florence, burial place of Michelangelo, Galileo and Machiavelli.
description: Santa Croce was begun in 1294 for the Franciscan friars, who needed a vast hall for preaching to the crowds of Florence; Vasari attributed the design to Arnolfo di Cambio. Its wide nave, lined by octagonal piers and covered with an open timber roof, gives a broad, airy space quite different from the vaulted cathedrals of France. Rich Florentine families endowed its chapels, which Giotto and his followers decorated with frescoes, among them Giotto's scenes of Saint Francis in the Bardi Chapel. Brunelleschi's Pazzi Chapel stands in the cloister. Santa Croce holds the tombs or memorials of Michelangelo, Galileo, Machiavelli, Rossini and Dante (whose body remains in Ravenna), and its neo-Gothic marble façade was added only in 1857–63. The flood of 1966 caused grave damage, including to Cimabue's crucifix.

title: Dome of Florence Cathedral
creator: brunelleschi
location: Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence, Italy
note: Brunelleschi's octagonal brick dome, built without centring, the engineering triumph of the early Renaissance.
description: By 1418 the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore had an octagonal crossing some 42 metres across, but no one knew how to roof it: there was not enough timber for the usual centring, and the design forbade external buttresses. Brunelleschi won the commission and built the dome between 1420 and 1436, the largest masonry dome ever built. It has two shells, an inner and an outer, linked by ribs and horizontal rings of stone and timber chains, and its bricks are laid in a herringbone pattern that held each course in place while the mortar set, so that the dome supported itself as it rose. He also invented hoisting machines, including a reversible ox-driven hoist, to raise some 37,000 tonnes of material. The marble lantern was completed after his death to his design. The dome dominates Florence and inspired every great dome that followed, including Michelangelo's at St Peter's.
image_file: Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore – Il Duomo di Firenze.jpg
image_caption: Dome of Florence Cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence, Italy

title: Ospedale degli Innocenti
creator: brunelleschi
location: Piazza della Santissima Annunziata, Florence, Italy
note: A hospital for abandoned children whose arcaded loggia is often called the first Renaissance building.
description: The silk guild of Florence commissioned Brunelleschi in 1419 to design a hospital for foundlings, children abandoned by their parents. Its loggia on the square, with nine round arches on slender Corinthian columns of grey pietra serena against white walls, is governed by a simple module: the spacing of the columns equals their height and the depth of the loggia, so that each bay is a cube under a domical vault. The clarity and classical detail made it the manifesto of a new architecture. Between the arches are glazed terracotta roundels of swaddled infants added by Andrea della Robbia in the 1480s. The institution cared for children for centuries; a revolving wheel, the ruota, allowed babies to be left anonymously until 1875. It still houses child welfare organisations and a museum.
image_file: Florence, Piazza SS Annunziata with Ospedale degli Innocenti (1419-39) and part of SS Annunziata (1601).jpg
image_caption: Ospedale degli Innocenti, Piazza della Santissima Annunziata, Florence, Italy

title: Pazzi Chapel
creator: brunelleschi
note: A chapter house of perfect geometry, a model of early Renaissance harmony.
description: The Pazzi family commissioned a chapter house for the friars of Santa Croce, set at the end of the first cloister. It is traditionally attributed to Brunelleschi, though it was completed long after his death and some scholars argue that others, perhaps Michelozzo or Giuliano da Maiano, designed part of it, especially the porch. The interior is a rectangle covered by a ribbed dome on pendentives, with a small square altar space under its own dome, and every surface is articulated by grey stone pilasters, arches and circles against white plaster. Glazed terracotta roundels of the apostles by Luca della Robbia and the evangelists add colour. The chapel is a three-dimensional diagram of the proportional thinking that defined Renaissance architecture.
image_file: Florence, Santa Croce, Cappella dei Pazzi, 1440s-70s.jpg
image_caption: Pazzi Chapel, Santa Croce, Florence, Italy

title: Palazzo Rucellai
creator: alberti
note: The first Renaissance palace façade with superimposed classical orders.
description: The merchant Giovanni Rucellai commissioned a new façade for his family's houses on the Via della Vigna Nuova, and it is generally attributed to Alberti, with Bernardo Rossellino as builder. For the first time since antiquity, a façade is articulated by three storeys of flat pilasters with entablatures, a sequence derived from the Colosseum, over a smooth, gently rusticated wall. Paired windows sit between the pilasters, and a heavy cornice crowns the top. The base imitates the diamond-pattern opus reticulatum of Roman walls. The façade was apparently left unfinished, its right edge still ragged. Its systematic use of the orders on a domestic building became a model for Renaissance palaces, especially in Rome.
image_file: Via della Vigna Nuova 18, palazzo rucellai, 02,0.jpg
image_caption: Palazzo Rucellai, Florence, Italy

title: Façade of Santa Maria Novella
creator: alberti
note: Alberti's geometric marble façade, which reconciled Gothic beginnings with classical proportion.
description: The Dominican church of Santa Maria Novella was built in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and its façade had been begun in Gothic style with marble arches and tomb niches. Giovanni Rucellai paid for its completion to Alberti's design, and his name is inscribed in the frieze. Alberti kept the Gothic lower parts but added a classical portal, a tall attic and a pediment-crowned upper storey linked to the lower by great scrolls, or volutes, that hide the aisle roofs, an invention imitated on hundreds of churches. The whole façade is based on squares and simple ratios. The inlaid white and green marble belongs to the Tuscan Romanesque tradition of San Miniato. Inside, the church holds Masaccio's Trinity and frescoes by Ghirlandaio.
image_caption: Façade of Santa Maria Novella, Florence, Italy

title: Sant'Andrea, Mantua
creator: alberti
note: Alberti's last design, a vast barrel-vaulted church modelled on Roman triumphal arches and basilicas.
description: Ludovico Gonzaga, marquis of Mantua, commissioned Alberti to design a church to house a relic of Christ's blood, and building began in 1472, the year of Alberti's death. Alberti replaced aisles with a single, huge barrel-vaulted nave lined by alternating large chapels and smaller piers, a rhythm repeated on the façade, which combines a temple front with a triumphal arch. The coffered vault deliberately evokes Roman baths and basilicas. Construction continued for centuries: the dome by Filippo Juvarra was completed in the eighteenth century. The single-nave, chapel-lined plan anticipated the Gesù in Rome and Counter-Reformation churches. The painter Andrea Mantegna is buried in one of its chapels.
image_caption: Sant'Andrea, Mantua, Mantua, Italy

title: Tempietto of San Pietro in Montorio
creator: bramante
note: A small round temple marking the traditional site of Saint Peter's martyrdom, the emblem of the High Renaissance.
description: The Tempietto, 'little temple', stands in the cloister of San Pietro in Montorio on the Janiculum, on the spot where tradition held that Saint Peter was crucified. It was commissioned by Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain; its date is debated, though an inscription gives 1502. Bramante based it on round Roman temples such as that at Tivoli: a cylindrical cella ringed by sixteen Tuscan Doric columns, a balustrade, a drum and a hemispherical dome, with a crypt below. Only about four and a half metres across inside, it has a monumental gravity. Bramante planned a circular colonnaded courtyard around it, which was not built but is known from Serlio's treatise. Serlio published it, and Palladio included it in his Four Books as the only modern building among the ancient temples; it inspired domes such as that of St Paul's.

title: St Peter's Basilica
creator: michelangelo
note: The mother church of Catholicism, rebuilt over 120 years by Bramante, Michelangelo, Maderno and others.
description: In 1506 Pope Julius II laid the foundation stone of a new St Peter's to replace the fourth-century basilica built by Constantine over the apostle's tomb. Bramante's plan was a Greek cross under a great dome. After his death in 1514, Raphael, Peruzzi and Antonio da Sangallo the Younger changed it repeatedly, until Michelangelo, appointed in 1546, simplified and unified the design, built most of the drum, and designed the ribbed double-shelled dome, which Giacomo della Porta and Domenico Fontana completed in 1588–90. Under Paul V, Carlo Maderno extended the nave into a Latin cross and added the façade, and the church was consecrated in 1626. Bernini then designed the baldachin, the Cathedra Petri and the square. The largest church in the world when built, it was financed partly by the sale of indulgences, which helped provoke the Reformation.
image_file: Basilica di San Pietro in Vaticano September 2015-1a.jpg
image_caption: St Peter's Basilica, Vatican City

title: Laurentian Library
creator: michelangelo
note: The Medici library whose vestibule and staircase are a manifesto of Mannerist architecture.
description: Pope Clement VII, a Medici, commissioned Michelangelo in 1524 to design a library for the family's manuscripts above the cloister of San Lorenzo. The long reading room, with its carved wooden desks and ceiling, is calm and orderly. The vestibule, or ricetto, is the opposite: a tall, cramped space where paired columns are sunk into the walls, consoles hang below them supporting nothing, and blind windows frame no view. From the floor a staircase seems to flow down like lava, its central flight of curved steps flanked by two straight ones. Michelangelo left Florence in 1534, and Vasari and Ammannati completed the staircase from his model, in grey pietra serena. The vestibule's deliberate breaking of classical rules made it one of the most influential rooms of the Renaissance.
image_caption: Laurentian Library, San Lorenzo, Florence, Italy

title: Piazza del Campidoglio
creator: michelangelo
note: Michelangelo's redesign of the Capitoline Hill, the first modern civic square planned as a whole.
description: In 1538 Pope Paul III had the ancient bronze equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius moved to the Capitoline Hill, the ancient centre of Rome and seat of the city government, and Michelangelo designed a new square around it. He set the statue on a pedestal at the centre of a trapezoidal piazza paved with an oval star pattern, rising slightly in the middle. He gave new façades to the medieval Palazzo dei Conservatori and Palazzo Senatorio and designed a matching Palazzo Nuovo opposite, all using a 'giant order' of pilasters rising through two storeys, and a ramped stair, the Cordonata, leading up from the city. Most of the work was carried out after his death, and the pavement was laid only in 1940. The palaces house the Capitoline Museums, the oldest public museum in the world, and the original statue is now indoors.
image_caption: Piazza del Campidoglio, Capitoline Hill, Rome, Italy

title: Palazzo Te
creator: giulio-romano
note: Giulio Romano's pleasure palace for Federico Gonzaga, the masterpiece of Mannerist architecture and illusion.
description: Federico II Gonzaga built the Palazzo Te on an island at the edge of Mantua, where his family had stables, as a villa for leisure and for meeting his mistress. Giulio Romano designed the building and its decoration. A low, square building around a courtyard, it plays with classical rules: in the courtyard, triglyphs drop out of the frieze as if slipping, rough and smooth stone alternate, and keystones project unexpectedly, jokes intended for viewers who knew the rules. Inside, frescoes by Giulio and his workshop include the Sala di Psiche, with erotic scenes from the story of Cupid and Psyche, and the Sala dei Giganti, painted from floor to vaulted ceiling with Jupiter's thunderbolts striking down giants as columns collapse around the viewer. It is now a museum.
image_caption: Palazzo Te, Mantua, Italy

title: Villa La Rotonda
creator: palladio
note: A square villa with four temple porticoes and a central dome, the most imitated house in the world.
description: Paolo Almerico, a retired cleric of the papal court, asked Palladio for a residence on a hilltop just outside Vicenza. Palladio designed a perfectly symmetrical square block with an identical Ionic temple portico on each side, each with a broad flight of steps, around a central round hall under a dome, so that every side commands a view of the surrounding countryside. He described it in his Four Books not as a farm villa but as a suburban house for pleasure, set like a theatre in the landscape. After Palladio's death Vincenzo Scamozzi completed it with a lower dome than first planned. The Rotonda was copied at Chiswick House and Mereworth Castle in England and at Monticello and many other houses in America. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Vicenza and the Palladian villas.
image_caption: Villa La Rotonda, Vicenza, Italy

title: Basilica Palladiana
creator: palladio
note: Palladio's two-storey marble loggias around Vicenza's medieval town hall, which made his name.
description: The Palazzo della Ragione, Vicenza's fifteenth-century town hall, had a vast hall on the upper floor covered by a keel-shaped roof, but its surrounding loggias collapsed in 1496. After several architects had been consulted, the young Palladio won the commission in 1549 to rebuild them. He wrapped the irregular medieval building in two storeys of arcades, Doric below and Ionic above, using the motif of an arch flanked by two narrow openings under a lintel, ever since called the Palladian or Serlian window. By varying the width of the small side openings, he absorbed the irregular spacing of the old building while keeping the arches uniform. Palladio called the building a basilica after the Roman halls of justice. It was completed after his death and is the centrepiece of Vicenza.
image_file: Basilica Palladiana (Vicenza) - facade on Piazza dei signori.jpg
image_caption: Basilica Palladiana, Piazza dei Signori, Vicenza, Italy

title: Il Redentore
creator: palladio
note: A votive church built after the plague of 1575–77, with a façade of interlocking temple fronts.
description: During a plague that killed perhaps a third of Venice's population, the Senate vowed in 1576 to build a church dedicated to Christ the Redeemer, and Palladio was chosen to design it on the island of Giudecca, run by Capuchin friars. Its white façade, facing the city across the Giudecca canal, interlocks a tall temple front with a lower, wider one, a solution for adapting a temple front to a church with a high nave and lower side chapels. Inside, a single nave with side chapels leads to a domed crossing and a choir screened by a curved row of columns, with the friars' choir beyond, reached through clear spatial stages. Every July, during the Festa del Redentore, a pontoon bridge is built across the canal so that Venetians can walk to the church, as the doge once did.
image_file: Chiesa del Santissimo Redentore, Venice, Italy.jpg
image_caption: Il Redentore, Giudecca, Venice, Italy

title: Church of the Gesù
creator: vignola
note: The mother church of the Jesuits, the model for Counter-Reformation churches worldwide.
description: Cardinal Alessandro Farnese funded the main church of the Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius of Loyola, and Vignola designed it in 1568. The Jesuits required a church in which large congregations could see the altar and hear sermons. Vignola gave it a single wide barrel-vaulted nave with side chapels instead of aisles, a short transept and a dome over the crossing that lights the altar. After Vignola's death in 1573 Giacomo della Porta completed it with a different façade, two storeys linked by scrolls, which was widely imitated. In the late seventeenth century Giovanni Battista Gaulli painted the ceiling with the Triumph of the Name of Jesus, figures and clouds appearing to burst into the church, and Andrea Pozzo designed the altar of Saint Ignatius. The Gesù became the pattern for Jesuit churches across Europe, Latin America and Asia.
image_caption: Church of the Gesù, Rome, Italy

title: El Escorial
creator: herrera
location: San Lorenzo de El Escorial, near Madrid, Spain
note: Philip II's monastery-palace in the mountains, an austere monument of Counter-Reformation Spain.
description: Philip II founded the monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial to commemorate the Spanish victory over France at Saint-Quentin in 1557 and to serve as a burial place for his father Charles V and his dynasty. Juan Bautista de Toledo drew up the plan, a vast rectangle of courtyards, and after his death Juan de Herrera completed the work. Built of grey granite with little ornament, it combines a monastery, a basilica with a dome, a royal palace, a library, a college and a pantheon of kings, where most Spanish monarchs since Charles V are buried. Philip governed his empire from a modest suite beside the basilica's high altar. The library has frescoed vaults and important manuscripts. El Escorial expressed the Catholic piety and imperial power of Habsburg Spain and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_file: Monasterio de El Escorial en Madrid.jpg
image_caption: El Escorial, San Lorenzo de El Escorial, near Madrid, Spain

title: Queen's House
creator: inigo-jones
note: The first consistently classical building in England, inspired by Palladio's villas.
description: Anne of Denmark, wife of James I, commissioned Inigo Jones in 1616 to build a house at Greenwich, straddling the road from London to Dover between the palace gardens and the park. Work stopped at her death in 1619 and was completed in 1635 for Queen Henrietta Maria, wife of Charles I. The white, cubic house, with a loggia facing the park, a terrace and simple proportioned windows, must have appeared astonishing beside the red-brick Tudor palace. Its central hall is a perfect cube of 40 feet, and the Tulip Stairs form the first geometrical, self-supporting spiral staircase in Britain. The house was later the centrepiece of Wren's Royal Hospital, whose layout kept the view to it open. It is part of the National Maritime Museum.
image_caption: Queen's House, Greenwich, London, England

title: Banqueting House, Whitehall
creator: inigo-jones
note: The only surviving part of Whitehall Palace, with a ceiling painted by Rubens.
description: James I commissioned Inigo Jones to build a new Banqueting House in the Palace of Whitehall, for court ceremonies and the masques Jones himself designed. Its façade, with Ionic and Corinthian orders in Portland stone, is modelled on Palladian palaces. Inside, a double cube hall, 110 by 55 feet, has a gallery and a flat ceiling divided into panels, which Charles I commissioned Peter Paul Rubens to paint with an allegory of the wise rule of his father, installed in 1636. Masques were stopped to protect the paintings from candle smoke. On 30 January 1649 Charles I walked through the hall to a scaffold outside a window, where he was executed. The rest of the palace burned in 1698, and the Banqueting House alone survives.
image_caption: Banqueting House, Whitehall, Whitehall, London, England

title: St Peter's Square
creator: bernini
note: Bernini's oval colonnades, which embrace the crowd before St Peter's like the arms of the Church.
description: Pope Alexander VII commissioned Bernini to create a square in front of St Peter's large enough for the crowds receiving the papal blessing. Bernini designed a trapezoidal space opening onto a vast oval, framed by two curved colonnades four columns deep, with 284 Doric columns and 140 statues of saints along the top. He compared the colonnades to the motherly arms of the Church welcoming believers and heretics alike. The Egyptian obelisk raised by Domenico Fontana in 1586 stands at the centre between two fountains, and discs set in the pavement mark points from which the rows of columns line up as one. A third arm closing the oval was never built, and Bernini's intended effect of surprise was altered when Mussolini's Via della Conciliazione cleared the old neighbourhood in front in the 1930s.
image_file: St Peter's Square, Vatican City - April 2007.jpg
image_caption: St Peter's Square, Vatican City

title: Sant'Andrea al Quirinale
creator: bernini
note: A small oval church which Bernini considered his most perfect architectural work.
description: Cardinal Camillo Pamphilj paid for this church for the Jesuit novitiate on the Quirinal Hill, opposite the papal palace. Bernini set an oval plan across the short axis, so the visitor enters on the long side and faces the altar directly across a short space, with the side chapels arranged around. The interior is clad in dark, richly coloured marble below and white and gold above, where a coffered dome lit from hidden windows rises. Above the altar, a painting of Saint Andrew's martyrdom, lit from a hidden source, is crowned by a sculpture of the saint rising through a broken pediment toward heaven, uniting painting, sculpture and architecture in a single drama. Bernini's son reported that his father sat there in old age, taking pleasure in the work.
image_caption: Sant'Andrea al Quirinale, Rome, Italy

title: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane
creator: borromini
note: Borromini's tiny church of undulating walls and an oval coffered dome, a masterpiece of Baroque geometry.
description: The Spanish Trinitarian order commissioned Borromini to build a monastery and church on a cramped corner site at the Quattro Fontane crossroads. The whole church could fit inside one of the piers of St Peter's dome. Its plan is generated from two equilateral triangles and an oval, producing walls that ripple in and out, with columns that are set close and continuous. Above, pendentives carry an oval dome whose coffers of crosses, octagons and hexagons diminish in size toward the lantern, so that the dome seems higher than it is, all in white stucco. The façade, his last work, completed after his death, undulates concave-convex-concave below and concave above. The church made Borromini famous; visitors from across Europe asked for its plans.
image_file: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane - Front.jpg
image_caption: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane, Rome, Italy

title: Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza
creator: borromini
note: The chapel of Rome's university, with a star-shaped plan and a spiralling lantern.
description: Borromini was given the church at the end of the courtyard of the Sapienza, the university of Rome, whose existing two-storey arcades he had to respect. His plan is based on a six-pointed star formed by two triangles, with alternating concave and convex-ended apses, an emblem associated with wisdom and with the bee of Pope Urban VIII's family, the Barberini. From the floor, the pattern rises unbroken into a white dome, with no drum, to the lantern. Outside, the concave façade continues the courtyard, and over it rise a stepped drum and a lantern that twists in a spiral like a corkscrew, topped by a flame and a crown. It is one of the most original buildings in Rome and has been compared to the spiralling towers of ancient legend.
image_caption: Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza, Rome, Italy

title: Vaux-le-Vicomte
creator: le-vau
note: Fouquet's château and gardens, where Le Vau, Le Brun and Le Nôtre first worked together.
description: Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's superintendent of finances, built Vaux-le-Vicomte south-east of Paris with Le Vau as architect, Charles Le Brun as painter and decorator, and André Le Nôtre as garden designer. Surrounded by a moat, the château centres on an oval domed salon facing the garden, and Le Nôtre's formal gardens, with parterres, terraces, canals and statues, stretch along an axis as far as the eye can see, using optical effects to hide changes in level. On 17 August 1661 Fouquet held a lavish fête for the young king. Three weeks later he was arrested for embezzlement and spent the rest of his life in prison, and Louis employed the same team at Versailles. The château remains in private hands and is open to visitors.
image_caption: Vaux-le-Vicomte, Maincy, Seine-et-Marne, France

title: Palace of Versailles
creator: le-vau
note: Louis XIV's palace, gardens and court, the model of royal magnificence for all Europe.
description: Louis XIII had a hunting lodge at Versailles, and from 1661 his son Louis XIV began transforming it. Le Vau wrapped the old brick château in a stone envelope from 1668, with a terrace facing the gardens. From 1678 Jules Hardouin-Mansart enlarged the palace, filling the terrace with the Hall of Mirrors and adding long north and south wings, and in 1682 the king moved the court and government there. Le Brun directed the decoration and Le Nôtre laid out the vast gardens with their parterres, fountains and Grand Canal. The palace became an instrument of rule, where nobles were kept close to the king in an elaborate etiquette. The Revolution forced Louis XVI to leave in 1789; Louis-Philippe made it a museum of French history in 1837, and the treaty ending the First World War was signed there in 1919.
image_caption: Palace of Versailles, Versailles, France

title: Hall of Mirrors
creator: hardouin-mansart
note: The great gallery of Versailles, lined with 357 mirrors facing tall windows onto the gardens.
description: Hardouin-Mansart replaced Le Vau's garden terrace with a gallery 73 metres long, completed in 1684. Seventeen arched windows overlooking the gardens are matched on the opposite wall by seventeen arches filled with 357 mirrors, a luxury made in France to compete with Venetian glass. Charles Le Brun painted the vaulted ceiling with thirty scenes glorifying Louis XIV's reign and victories, and the gallery originally held solid silver furniture, melted down in 1689 to pay for war. It was used for daily passage, court festivities and receptions of ambassadors. The German Empire was proclaimed there in 1871, and the Treaty of Versailles was signed there in 1919. A major restoration was completed in 2007.
image_caption: Hall of Mirrors, Palace of Versailles, France

title: Les Invalides (Dôme des Invalides)
creator: hardouin-mansart
note: The gilded domed church of the hospital for old soldiers, where Napoleon is buried.
description: Louis XIV founded the Hôtel des Invalides in 1670 to house disabled and aged soldiers, and Libéral Bruant built its courtyards and soldiers' church. In 1677 Hardouin-Mansart was commissioned to add a royal chapel joined to the soldiers' church, completed in 1706. It is a centrally planned church under a dome, with a two-storey columned façade, and the dome has three shells: an inner one open at the top, through which one sees a painted second dome lit by hidden windows, and an outer timber and lead dome rising to a gilded lantern 107 metres high. Admired as the finest French classical dome, it was regilded in 1989. In 1840 Napoleon's remains were returned from Saint Helena, and Louis Visconti designed his red quartzite tomb in a crypt under the dome, completed in 1861.
image_file: Hôtel des Invalides from the Eiffel Tower, 23 July 2009.jpg
image_caption: Les Invalides (Dôme des Invalides), Paris, France

title: St Paul's Cathedral
creator: wren
note: Wren's domed cathedral, rebuilt after the Great Fire of London, a symbol of the city.
description: Old St Paul's, a huge Gothic cathedral, was gutted in the Great Fire of 1666. Wren's first designs, including a Greek-cross 'Great Model', were rejected by the clergy, and his approved design of 1675 was a Latin-cross plan, which he altered as he built. The cathedral was completed in 1710, the first in England built by a single architect in his lifetime. Its dome, inspired by St Peter's and Bramante's Tempietto, consists of three parts: a low inner dome seen from inside, a brick cone that carries the stone lantern, and an outer timber dome covered with lead. Wren used screen walls along the upper aisles to hide the flying buttresses. The cathedral survived the Blitz in 1940, an image of defiance, and has been the scene of state funerals, jubilees and royal weddings.
image_caption: St Paul's Cathedral, City of London, England

title: Old Royal Naval College (Royal Hospital for Seamen)
creator: wren
note: Wren's Baroque hospital for retired sailors, framing the view to the Queen's House.
description: In 1694 Queen Mary II founded a hospital for disabled and retired seamen on the site of the old Tudor palace at Greenwich, and Wren gave his services free. Because the queen insisted on keeping the view from the river to Inigo Jones's Queen's House, Wren designed two pairs of courts separated by a broad avenue, with twin domes and colonnades over the Painted Hall and the chapel. Nicholas Hawksmoor and John Vanbrugh continued the work. James Thornhill painted the Painted Hall from 1707 to 1726, a vast celebration of Protestant monarchy and naval power. The hospital closed in 1869, and the buildings became the Royal Naval College in 1873; since 1998 they have housed the University of Greenwich and Trinity Laban. With the park and observatory they form the Maritime Greenwich World Heritage Site.
image_file: Royal Naval College Greenwich view from the Thames.jpg
image_caption: Old Royal Naval College (Royal Hospital for Seamen), Greenwich, London, England

title: Karlskirche
creator: fischer-von-erlach
note: A Baroque votive church with an oval dome flanked by two Trajanic columns.
description: During the plague of 1713, Emperor Charles VI vowed a church to his patron saint, Charles Borromeo, and Fischer von Erlach won the competition to design it. After his death in 1723 his son Joseph Emanuel completed it, modifying the design. The façade combines a classical temple portico, an oval dome on a high drum and two giant columns modelled on Trajan's Column, wound with reliefs of the saint's life, flanked by low pavilions. The columns also recalled the Pillars of Hercules on the Habsburg emblem and the Temple of Solomon, so that the church brought together Rome, Jerusalem and imperial power. Inside, the oval dome is painted with frescoes by Johann Michael Rottmayr. The church, which faces Karlsplatz, is a symbol of Vienna.
image_caption: Karlskirche, Vienna, Austria

title: Würzburg Residence
creator: neumann
note: A great Baroque palace with Neumann's vaulted staircase and Tiepolo's ceiling fresco of the four continents.
description: The Schönborn prince-bishops of Würzburg, rich and ambitious rulers in Franconia, built the Residence from 1720 with Balthasar Neumann in charge, consulting leading architects from Paris and Vienna such as Robert de Cotte, Germain Boffrand and Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt. Around a forecourt are long wings with five courtyards, and the interiors include the Imperial Hall, the court chapel and the Mirror Cabinet. The highlight is the staircase, roofed by a single vault some 18 by 30 metres without supports, a daring structure that critics predicted would collapse. In 1752–53 Giovanni Battista Tiepolo painted it with an allegory of Apollo and the four continents, among the largest frescoes ever made. The vault survived Allied bombing in 1945, which destroyed much of the palace and city; the palace was restored and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_caption: Würzburg Residence, Würzburg, Germany

title: Basilica of the Fourteen Holy Helpers (Vierzehnheiligen)
creator: neumann
note: A Rococo pilgrimage church of interlocking ovals, flooded with light, white and gold.
description: Vierzehnheiligen, on a hillside above the Main valley, marks the place where a shepherd reported visions of the Christ Child and the Fourteen Holy Helpers, saints invoked against disease and misfortune, in 1445–46. The Cistercian abbey of Langheim commissioned a new pilgrimage church, and after another architect had begun building in the wrong place, Neumann took over in 1743. He had to keep the altar of the apparition in the middle of the nave, and designed a plan of interlocking ovals that places it at the heart of the church. The interior, decorated by the Feichtmayr and Übelherr workshops with stucco, and with frescoes by Giuseppe Appiani, is white, pink and gold, with abundant windows. The free-standing altar of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, shaped like a Rococo carriage or coral reef, is the focus of pilgrimage to this day.
image_caption: Basilica of the Fourteen Holy Helpers (Vierzehnheiligen), Bad Staffelstein, Bavaria, Germany

title: Winter Palace
creator: rastrelli
note: The vast green-and-white residence of the Russian tsars, now the main building of the Hermitage.
description: Empress Elizabeth commissioned Rastrelli to build a new Winter Palace on the Neva, the fourth on the site. Completed in 1762, just after her death, it is a four-sided block around a courtyard, with over a thousand rooms and façades on the river and Palace Square, punctuated by columns, window surrounds and statues on the roofline. Rastrelli's Jordan Staircase survived a fire in 1837, after which much of the interior was rebuilt by Vasily Stasov and Alexander Bryullov. The palace was the main residence of the tsars until 1904, the scene of the massacre of Bloody Sunday in 1905, and in October 1917 the seat of the Provisional Government stormed by the Bolsheviks. It is now part of the State Hermitage Museum, founded on Catherine the Great's collection.
image_caption: Winter Palace, Palace Square, St Petersburg, Russia

title: Panthéon (Church of Sainte-Geneviève)
creator: soufflot
note: Soufflot's Neoclassical church that the Revolution turned into a temple for France's great men and women.
description: Louis XV vowed during an illness in 1744 to rebuild the abbey church of Sainte-Geneviève, the patron saint of Paris, and Soufflot's design was chosen in 1755. It is a Greek cross with a dome over the crossing on a high colonnaded drum, approached through a giant Corinthian portico modelled on the Pantheon in Rome. Inside, Soufflot used freestanding columns carrying straight entablatures and light vaults, seeking to combine the lightness of Gothic and the purity of Greek architecture. Doubts about whether the piers could carry the dome led to controversy, and the piers were later reinforced. Finished in 1790, it was converted by the revolutionary government into a mausoleum for great Frenchmen, and windows were blocked to make it more sombre. It changed status several times in the nineteenth century; Voltaire, Rousseau, Victor Hugo, Marie Curie and others are buried there. Foucault demonstrated the earth's rotation with his pendulum there in 1851.
image_caption: Panthéon (Church of Sainte-Geneviève), Paris, France

title: Royal Saltworks at Arc-et-Senans
creator: ledoux
note: A royal salt factory laid out as an ideal semicircular community, an early monument of industrial architecture.
description: Salt was a royal monopoly and a valuable source of tax. Ledoux, as inspector of saltworks in Franche-Comté, designed a new works near the forest of Chaux, which supplied wood to fire the brine evaporation pans; the brine was piped from Salins. Buildings are arranged on a semicircle: the director's house at the centre, with a temple portico of columns banded with stone drums and a chapel, flanked by the two salt-boiling halls, and around the arc the houses of workers, coopers and blacksmiths, with gardens behind. The gatehouse is a grotto-like portico of heavy Doric columns, with carved urns spilling petrified salt water. The works operated until 1895. Ledoux later imagined it as the centre of an ideal city. Restored after the 1920s, it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_file: France arc et senas saline royal main building 1.jpg
image_caption: Royal Saltworks at Arc-et-Senans, Arc-et-Senans, Doubs, France

title: Monticello
creator: jefferson
note: Jefferson's hilltop house, rebuilt for decades, a Palladian and Neoclassical self-portrait.
description: Jefferson began building on his 'little mountain' near Charlottesville in 1769, following Palladio's books. After his years in Paris, where he admired the domed Hôtel de Salm, he largely demolished and rebuilt the house from 1796 to 1809, adding the octagonal dome over the west front, the first on an American house. Inside are his own inventions: a two-faced clock, a dumbwaiter and a revolving bookstand. Service rooms, kitchens and stables were placed in wings sunk into the hillside under terraces, so the house appears to stand alone; Mulberry Row along the slope held the workshops and dwellings of the enslaved people who built and ran the plantation, among them the Hemings family. The house appears on the US nickel. With the University of Virginia, it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_caption: Monticello, Charlottesville, Virginia, United States

title: The Rotunda and Lawn, University of Virginia
creator: jefferson
note: Jefferson's 'academical village', with a half-scale Pantheon as its library.
description: Jefferson conceived the University of Virginia as an 'academical village', a community of scholars instead of a single great building. A long terraced lawn is flanked by two rows of five pavilions, each a professor's house and classroom in a different classical order taken from ancient Roman examples, linked by colonnades in front of student rooms; behind are gardens and further ranges. At the head stands the Rotunda, the library, a half-scale version of the Pantheon in Rome, completed in 1826. Enslaved workers built much of it. Its brick and white-columned style became the model of American campuses. The Rotunda burned in 1895 and was rebuilt by Stanford White, and was later restored to Jefferson's design. In 1976 members of the American Institute of Architects voted it the proudest achievement of American architecture of the previous two hundred years.
image_caption: The Rotunda and Lawn, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, Virginia, United States

title: Altes Museum
creator: schinkel
note: One of the first purpose-built public museums, fronted by a long Ionic colonnade.
description: King Frederick William III of Prussia agreed to open the royal collections to the public, and Schinkel designed a museum facing the royal palace across the Lustgarten. Its façade is a single colonnade of eighteen Ionic columns raised on a podium, recalling a Greek stoa. Behind it, a two-storey rotunda modelled on the Pantheon, lined with ancient statues, forms the heart of the building, with galleries for sculpture on the ground floor and paintings above around two courtyards. An open staircase between the columns let visitors look back over the city. It opened in 1830 and was the first building on what became Museum Island, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Damaged in the Second World War, it was restored and today shows the classical antiquities collection.
image_caption: Altes Museum, Museum Island, Berlin, Germany

title: Sir John Soane's Museum
creator: soane
note: Soane's house, office and museum, a labyrinth of top-lit rooms crammed with antiquities and art.
description: Soane bought and rebuilt three adjoining houses on Lincoln's Inn Fields between 1792 and 1824, turning them into a home, an office for his practice and a museum for his students. Behind a façade with a projecting loggia of Portland stone, small rooms open into each other through arches, shafts and domes, lit from above by coloured glass and multiplied by convex mirrors. Casts, fragments, models, drawings and urns cover the walls, around a domed space and a crypt containing the sarcophagus of the Egyptian pharaoh Seti I, bought in 1824. A picture room with hinged panels holds Hogarth's series A Rake's Progress and An Election, as well as paintings by Canaletto and Turner. An Act of Parliament of 1833 preserved the house as Soane left it, free to visitors, and so it remains.

title: Palace of Westminster
creator: barry
note: The Gothic Revival Houses of Parliament by Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin.
description: Most of the old Palace of Westminster burned in October 1834; only Westminster Hall, the crypt and the Jewel Tower survived. A competition required a design in Gothic or Elizabethan style, and Barry's won in 1836. He organised the new palace, about 300 metres along the Thames, around a central lobby between the House of Lords and the House of Commons, with long corridors and courtyards, while Augustus Pugin designed the Perpendicular Gothic detail, the tiles, wallpapers, furniture, stained glass and metalwork. The House of Lords opened in 1847 and the Commons in 1852; work continued until 1870. The Victoria Tower and the clock tower, now the Elizabeth Tower, frame the skyline. Bombed in 1941, the Commons chamber was rebuilt by Giles Gilbert Scott. With Westminster Abbey it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and a major restoration is planned.
image_file: Palace of Westminster as seen from Westminster Bridge.jpg
image_caption: Palace of Westminster, Westminster, London, England

title: Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben)
creator: pugin
note: Pugin's clock tower for the Houses of Parliament, his last design and a symbol of London.
description: The great clock tower at the north end of the Palace of Westminster, known as the Clock Tower until 2012 and now as the Elizabeth Tower, was designed by Pugin in 1852, the last major design before his breakdown and death; he based it on an earlier tower he had designed. About 96 metres high, it is of brick clad in stone, with a cast-iron spire. The clock mechanism, designed by Edmund Beckett Denison and built by Edward John Dent and his stepson, began keeping time in 1859 and was famous for its accuracy. The name Big Ben properly belongs to the largest bell, which cracked soon after installation and was given a quarter turn so its hammer would strike elsewhere. A restoration was completed in 2022.
image_file: Elizabeth Tower and the north front of the Palace of Westminster, London.jpg
image_caption: Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben), Palace of Westminster, London, England

title: St Giles' Catholic Church, Cheadle
creator: pugin
note: Pugin's 'perfect Cheadle', a parish church in which every surface is decorated.
description: John Talbot, 16th Earl of Shrewsbury, the richest English Catholic, funded a parish church at Cheadle near his estate at Alton Towers, and Pugin was given a free hand. He designed it in the Decorated Gothic style of the early fourteenth century, which he considered the purest, with a tall spire visible across the countryside. Inside, every surface is coloured and gilded: the walls stencilled with patterns, the floor tiled by Minton, the screen and the Easter sepulchre carved, the windows filled with stained glass by William Wailes, the metalwork by John Hardman. Pugin called it 'perfect Cheadle', and it remains the most complete expression of his ideal of a revived medieval parish church.
image_file: St Giles RC Church Cheadle Staffs tower.jpg
image_caption: St Giles' Catholic Church, Cheadle, Cheadle, Staffordshire, England

title: Château de Pierrefonds
creator: viollet-le-duc
note: A ruined medieval castle rebuilt by Viollet-le-Duc for Napoleon III, an imaginative restoration.
description: Pierrefonds was built around 1400 by Louis of Orléans, brother of Charles VI, and dismantled on the orders of Cardinal Richelieu in 1617. Napoleon III, who visited the ruins, commissioned Viollet-le-Duc in 1857 to restore part of it as a residence, and the project expanded into a full reconstruction.
