Viollet-le-Duc rebuilt walls, towers, machicolations and battlements according to his understanding of medieval military architecture, but the interiors, with painted decoration and carvings, are a nineteenth-century fantasy. Work stopped after the fall of the Second Empire in 1870 and finished after his death. Pierrefonds is a textbook case of the restoration philosophy of its architect, admired for its imagination and criticised for inventing rather than preserving.
image_file: Château de Pierrefonds vu depuis le Parc.jpg
image_caption: Château de Pierrefonds, Pierrefonds, Oise, France

title: The Crystal Palace
creator: paxton
location: Hyde Park, London; moved to Sydenham, destroyed 1936
note: The prefabricated iron and glass hall of the Great Exhibition of 1851.
description: The Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations, promoted by Prince Albert, needed a building that could be erected quickly and removed afterwards. Joseph Paxton's design, based on his glasshouses, was accepted in July 1850, and the contractors Fox, Henderson and Co. built it in Hyde Park in about nine months. It was about 563 metres long, made of standardised cast-iron columns and girders, timber and some 300,000 panes of glass, assembled from parts mass-produced off site, with a vaulted transept tall enough to enclose existing elm trees. Six million visitors came to see over 100,000 exhibits. The magazine Punch called it the Crystal Palace. It was rebuilt in enlarged form at Sydenham Hill in south London, where it served as a place of entertainment until it burned down in 1936.
image_file: Crystal Palace General view from Water Temple.jpg
image_caption: The Crystal Palace, Hyde Park, London; moved to Sydenham, destroyed 1936

title: Palais Garnier (Paris Opéra)
creator: garnier
note: The opera house of Second Empire Paris, a summit of Beaux-Arts splendour.
description: The opera house was a centrepiece of Baron Haussmann's rebuilding of Paris under Napoleon III. Charles Garnier, aged thirty-five, won the competition of 1861 from over 170 entrants. Construction was slowed by an underground water table, which was contained by a vast concrete tank, later the inspiration for the lake in Gaston Leroux's The Phantom of the Opera, and by the war of 1870–71 and the Commune, and the house opened in 1875. Each function has its own volume: the façade and loggia, the grand staircase and foyers, the horseshoe auditorium under a dome, and the huge stage house. Inside, coloured marbles, onyx, gilding, mosaics, mirrors and sculpture create a theatre of society in which the audience is on display. Marc Chagall painted a new auditorium ceiling in 1964. It remains a home of the Paris Opera Ballet.
image_file: Paris Opera full frontal architecture, May 2009.jpg
image_caption: Palais Garnier (Paris Opéra), Paris, France

title: Eiffel Tower
creator: eiffel
note: The 300-metre wrought-iron tower of the 1889 Exposition, the tallest structure in the world until 1930.
description: For the Exposition Universelle of 1889, celebrating the centenary of the Revolution, the government held a competition for a tower 300 metres high. Eiffel's company won with a design developed by its engineers Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier and the architect Stephen Sauvestre. About 18,000 wrought-iron parts, designed and prefabricated in the company's workshops, were joined with some 2.5 million rivets in just over two years. Four curved legs, shaped to resist the wind, rise to three platforms. Prominent artists and writers protested in 1887 against what they called a useless and monstrous tower. It was meant to stand only for twenty years, but its usefulness for radio transmission saved it. The tallest structure in the world until the Chrysler Building of 1930, it became the symbol of Paris and one of the most visited monuments in the world.

title: Wainwright Building
creator: sullivan
note: Sullivan's ten-storey office block, the first skyscraper to give the tall building a unified artistic form.
description: The brewer Ellis Wainwright commissioned Adler and Sullivan to design a ten-storey office building in St Louis on a steel frame. Sullivan treated the tall building as a whole: a two-storey base for shops, an attic crowning the top with a deep frieze of terracotta foliage and a cornice, and between them a shaft of continuous vertical piers rising uninterrupted, with recessed spandrels between the windows, so that the building appears to soar. Since not every pier contains a column, the design emphasises an image of verticality rather than a literal statement of structure. Frank Lloyd Wright called it the moment when the tall building became architecture. It was saved from demolition in the 1970s and restored as state government offices.
image_file: Wainwright Building, 7th Street and Chestnut Street, St. Louis, MO - 53051647915.jpg
image_caption: Wainwright Building, St Louis, Missouri, United States

title: Carson, Pirie, Scott and Company Building (Sullivan Center)
creator: sullivan
note: A department store with broad Chicago windows and a cast-iron entrance of luxuriant ornament.
description: Built for the Schlesinger and Mayer department store and soon taken over by Carson, Pirie, Scott and Company, the building on State Street was Sullivan's last large commission. The upper storeys express the steel frame directly as a grid of broad horizontal 'Chicago windows', each with a large fixed pane between narrow opening sashes, clad in white terracotta. At street level, where shoppers passed, the display windows are framed by intricate cast-iron ornament of foliage and geometric forms in Sullivan's personal style, swelling over the rounded corner entrance. The store was later extended by Daniel Burnham's firm and others. Carson's closed in 2007, and the building was restored and renamed the Sullivan Center, with offices and shops.
image_file: Carson, Pirie, Scott and Company Building (Sullivan Center), Chicago, Illinois (9179422705).jpg
image_caption: Carson, Pirie, Scott and Company Building (Sullivan Center), Chicago, Illinois, United States

title: Flatiron Building
creator: burnham
note: A steel-framed wedge of a skyscraper on a triangular site at Madison Square.
description: The Fuller Company commissioned D. H. Burnham and Company to design a twenty-two-storey office building on the triangular plot formed by Broadway and Fifth Avenue at 23rd Street. Its steel frame, one of the earliest in New York for so tall a building, is clad in limestone and terracotta, organised like a classical column into base, shaft and capital, with Renaissance ornament. The narrow point is only about two metres wide. The building's shape, likened to a clothes iron, gave it its popular name, and the wind gusts around it became a legend. Photographers such as Alfred Stieglitz and Edward Steichen made it an icon of the modern city. Long used as offices, it is undergoing conversion to apartments.
image_file: Edificio Fuller (Flatiron) en 2010 desde el Empire State crop boxin.jpg
image_caption: Flatiron Building, New York City, United States

title: Hôtel Tassel
creator: horta
note: A town house for a professor, generally regarded as the first Art Nouveau building.
description: Émile Tassel, a professor of descriptive geometry at the Free University of Brussels, commissioned his friend Victor Horta to build a house on a narrow plot in the Rue Paul-Émile Janson. Horta abandoned the conventional corridor plan of Brussels houses and arranged the rooms around an octagonal hall and a central staircase lit from above, with levels shifting by half-storeys. Exposed iron columns branch at the top like plant stems, and their whiplash curves continue in the painted walls, mosaic floor, stair rail and stained glass, all designed by Horta. The stone façade swells into a central bay window carried on iron. The house's unity of structure and ornament defined Art Nouveau. Divided into flats and altered in the twentieth century, it was restored in the 1980s and is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site with three other Horta houses.
image_caption: Hôtel Tassel, Brussels, Belgium

title: Sagrada Família
creator: gaudi
note: Gaudí's unfinished expiatory church, under construction since 1882 and Barcelona's emblem.
description: The Basílica de la Sagrada Família was begun in 1882 by a devotional association as an expiatory church funded by donations, to a Gothic Revival design by Francisco de Paula del Villar. Gaudí took over in 1883 and transformed it into a vast symbolic project: three façades representing the Nativity, the Passion and the Glory, eighteen spires for the apostles, the evangelists, the Virgin and Christ, and an interior forest of branching, tree-like columns. He worked on it for forty-three years, completing only the crypt, the apse walls and part of the Nativity façade. His workshop was burned and his models smashed in the Spanish Civil War, and their fragments were later pieced together. Construction resumed and, with computer design, has accelerated; the church was consecrated as a basilica in 2010 and the central tower of Jesus Christ, which makes it the tallest church in the world, was scheduled to be completed in 2026, the centenary of Gaudí's death. It is partly a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
image_caption: Sagrada Família, Barcelona, Spain

title: Casa Batlló
creator: gaudi
note: A remodelled town house with a shimmering mosaic façade and a roof like a dragon's back.
description: The textile industrialist Josep Batlló commissioned Gaudí to remodel his family's apartment building on Barcelona's fashionable Passeig de Gràcia. Gaudí added a new façade covered in broken ceramic and coloured glass, with balconies shaped like masks or skulls and bone-like columns at the lower floors, giving it the nickname of the house of bones. The roof's ridge of scaly glazed tiles has been read as the back of a dragon pierced by the cross-topped tower, an allusion to Saint George, the patron saint of Catalonia, though Gaudí left no explanation. Inside, the stair well is tiled in blues that grow paler toward the bottom to spread light evenly, and walls and ceilings curve without corners. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a museum.
image_file: Casa Batllo Overview Barcelona Spain cut.jpg
image_caption: Casa Batlló, Passeig de Gràcia, Barcelona, Spain

title: Casa Milà (La Pedrera)
creator: gaudi
note: An undulating stone apartment building, nicknamed the stone quarry, with a sculptural roof.
description: Pere Milà and his wife Roser Segimon commissioned Gaudí to build an apartment building on a corner of the Passeig de Gràcia. Its undulating limestone façade, with wrought-iron balconies like seaweed, earned it the mocking name La Pedrera, 'the stone quarry'. Inside, it has no load-bearing walls: a structure of stone and brick columns and steel beams allows the apartments to be divided freely, around two courtyards that bring in light. The attic is roofed by catenary brick arches, and on the roof terrace chimneys and ventilation towers stand like helmeted warriors. Gaudí left before completion after disputes with the owners. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984, it was restored by a savings bank foundation and is open to visitors.
image_caption: Casa Milà (La Pedrera), Passeig de Gràcia, Barcelona, Spain

title: Park Güell
creator: gaudi
note: A failed garden suburb that became a public park full of Gaudí's mosaic and stone fantasies.
description: Eusebi Güell bought a hillside above Barcelona to create a garden city of houses for the wealthy, on the English model, and commissioned Gaudí to design it. Only two houses were built and sold, one bought by Gaudí himself, and the project was abandoned; the city acquired the land as a park in 1926. Gaudí's infrastructure remains: gatehouses with mushroom-like roofs, a monumental stair with a mosaic salamander, a hall of eighty-six Doric columns intended as a market, supporting a great terrace above, edged by a serpentine bench covered in broken-tile mosaic made largely by Josep Maria Jujol, and paths carried on rough stone viaducts that merge with the hillside. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Glasgow School of Art (Mackintosh Building)
creator: mackintosh
note: Mackintosh's art school, a fusion of Scottish tradition and modern design, gutted by fire in 2014 and 2018.
description: Mackintosh won the competition for a new building for the Glasgow School of Art in 1896, and it was built in two phases, the east half in 1897–99 and the west in 1907–09, on a steep sloping site. The north front has huge studio windows for steady light, framed by stone and decorated with wrought-iron brackets and finials. The west wing is more severe and vertical, with tall oriel windows. Its library, of dark wood with suspended lamps and slender posts, was regarded as one of the finest interiors of its era. Mackintosh designed the furniture and fittings. A fire in 2014 destroyed the library, and as restoration neared completion a second fire in 2018 gutted the building. The school has committed to rebuilding it.

title: Austrian Postal Savings Bank
creator: otto-wagner
note: A bank whose façade is clad with marble plates held by visible bolts and whose glass-roofed hall anticipates modernism.
description: The Postsparkasse, the Austrian postal savings bank founded in 1883, held a competition for its headquarters on the Ringstrasse, won by Otto Wagner. The façade is clad in thin marble slabs fixed by aluminium-capped bolts that make the means of attachment visible, while aluminium figures and acroteria crown the cornice. The main banking hall has a glass ceiling carried on slender steel columns, with a glass floor bringing light to the level below, and aluminium heating ducts and fittings, then a new material, all designed by Wagner. The building expresses his argument that architecture should be shaped by modern needs and materials. It is still used by the bank and houses a museum.

title: Chrysler Building
creator: van-alen
location: Manhattan, New York City, United States
note: The Art Deco skyscraper with a stainless-steel crown, briefly the tallest building in the world.
description: Built for the automobile magnate Walter P. Chrysler, the building rose during the race for the tallest skyscraper in New York. To beat 40 Wall Street, Van Alen had a 38-metre spire assembled secretly inside the crown and raised into place in about ninety minutes in October 1929, bringing the height to 319 metres. It was the tallest building in the world for eleven months, until the Empire State Building. Its terraced crown of stainless-steel arches with triangular windows, its eagle-head gargoyles and its brickwork frieze of hubcaps celebrate the car and the machine age. The triangular lobby, with marble, chrome and a ceiling mural on the theme of transport, is one of the great Art Deco interiors.

title: Fagus Factory
creator: gropius
note: A shoe-last factory with glass curtain walls wrapping its corners, a founding work of modern architecture.
description: Carl Benscheidt, a manufacturer of shoe lasts, commissioned Walter Gropius and Adolf Meyer in 1911 to redesign the façade of his new factory, whose plan had already been drawn by another architect. Gropius and Meyer gave the main building walls of glass and steel set in front of the brick piers, and wrapped the glass around the corners without corner supports, so that the walls seem weightless. The building expressed a modern, light and healthy workplace, and its image was meant to advertise the company. Further buildings were added until 1925, including interiors in the early Bauhaus style. The factory is still in operation, making shoe lasts, and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011.

title: Bauhaus Building, Dessau
creator: gropius
note: The school building of the Bauhaus, a manifesto of functional modern architecture with a glass curtain wall.
description: When the Bauhaus left Weimar under political pressure in 1925, the industrial city of Dessau offered it a new home, and Gropius designed its building. It is a pinwheel of separate wings for separate functions: a workshop block with a continuous curtain wall of glass, a teaching wing, a bridge over the road housing the administration, an assembly hall and canteen, and a five-storey block of studio flats for students with small balconies. Its asymmetrical composition can only be grasped by walking around it, and the school's workshops made its lighting, furniture and lettering. The Nazis closed the Dessau Bauhaus in 1932. Damaged in the war and altered, the building was restored and is used again by the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Barcelona Pavilion
creator: mies
note: The German pavilion of the 1929 exposition, a flowing space of marble, glass and steel.
description: Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich designed the German Pavilion at the 1929 Barcelona International Exposition as a representational building with no exhibits, used for the opening ceremony with the Spanish king. A flat roof rests on eight cruciform chrome-clad steel columns, freeing walls of onyx, green marble and glass to stand as independent planes that guide visitors through a continuous space, with two shallow pools, one holding a bronze statue by Georg Kolbe. The Barcelona Chair was designed for the pavilion. It was dismantled in 1930, but its photographs made it one of the most influential buildings of the century. A permanent reconstruction was built on the original site in 1983–86.

title: Villa Tugendhat
creator: mies
note: A luxurious modernist villa with an open living space, an onyx wall and windows that sink into the floor.
description: Grete and Fritz Tugendhat, from wealthy industrial families, commissioned Mies to build a house on a sloping site overlooking Brno. From the street, it appears as a low single storey; on the garden side, the main floor opens as a single living space about 280 square metres in area, divided only by a wall of golden onyx and a curved wall of Macassar ebony, with chrome cruciform columns. Two huge glass panes could be lowered electrically into the floor. Mies and Lilly Reich designed the furniture, including the Tugendhat and Brno chairs. The family, who were Jewish, fled in 1938; the house was confiscated, damaged in the war, and used for other purposes. Restored and opened as a museum, it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Farnsworth House
creator: mies
note: A glass pavilion raised above a floodplain, the purest statement of Mies's 'less is more'.
description: Edith Farnsworth, a Chicago physician, commissioned Mies to design a weekend retreat on a wooded site beside the Fox River. The house is a single glass-walled room between a floor slab and a roof slab, held about 1.6 metres above the floodplain by eight white-painted steel columns welded to the edges, with a terrace and floating steps. A wooden core contains the kitchen, bathrooms and fireplace. The house became the subject of a lawsuit between architect and client over costs, and Farnsworth complained about living in a glass box. It has been flooded several times. Philip Johnson's Glass House was inspired by it. It is now a museum owned by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

title: Villa Savoye
creator: le-corbusier
note: Le Corbusier's white villa on pilotis, the summary of his five points of a new architecture.
description: Pierre and Eugénie Savoye commissioned a weekend house on a meadow at Poissy, and Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret designed it as a demonstration of the five points of a new architecture: pilotis lifting the house above the ground, a free plan, a free façade, ribbon windows and a roof garden. The ground floor, curved to follow the turning circle of a car, holds the entrance and service rooms; a ramp leads up to the main living floor around an open terrace and on to a sunroof sheltered by curving screens, an architectural promenade. The family suffered from leaks and found the house impractical, and it was nearly demolished after the war before André Malraux had it protected. Restored, it is open as a museum and is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing of Le Corbusier's works.

title: Frederick C. Robie House
creator: wright
location: Hyde Park, Chicago, Illinois, United States
note: The masterpiece of Wright's Prairie style, with long cantilevered roofs and a continuous interior.
description: Frederick Robie, a businessman who made bicycles and then car parts, commissioned Wright to design a house on a narrow corner lot near the University of Chicago. Wright stretched it horizontally, with long bands of Roman brick, low hipped roofs projecting far beyond the walls on steel beams and art-glass windows, so that it seems rooted in the flat prairie. The living and dining rooms form a single long space on the upper floor, divided only by a central fireplace, with doors onto balconies. Wright designed furniture, lighting and glass. The house was threatened with demolition several times, and its rescue in the 1950s and 1960s became an early landmark of preservation. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Wright's twentieth-century architecture.

title: Fallingwater
creator: wright
note: A house cantilevered over a waterfall, the most famous house of the twentieth century.
description: Edgar J. Kaufmann, a Pittsburgh department store owner, asked Wright for a weekend house near a waterfall on Bear Run, expecting a view of the falls. Wright placed the house over them, anchoring it to the rock with a stone chimney core from which reinforced-concrete terraces cantilever above the stream. Inside, flagstone floors, a boulder rising through the living room hearth and stone walls continue the landscape, and glass walls and corner windows open to the woods; a stair descends from the living room to the water. The cantilevers sagged over time and were reinforced with post-tensioning in 2002. Kaufmann's son gave the house to the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy in 1963. It is a museum and part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Wright's architecture.

title: Rietveld Schröder House
creator: rietveld
note: A small house of sliding planes and primary colours, the only building realised fully on De Stijl principles.
description: Truus Schröder-Schräder, a widow with three children, commissioned Rietveld to design a house at the end of a row of brick houses on the edge of Utrecht, and she took an active part in the design. The house is composed of planes, lines and coloured elements, white and grey walls, red, yellow, blue and black lines, that seem to slide apart, with balconies and roof slabs projecting beyond the walls. The ground floor has conventional rooms, but the upper floor can be opened as a single space or divided into rooms by sliding and folding partitions. Windows open at right angles to the façade so that the corner disappears. Schröder lived there until her death in 1985. It is a museum and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Paimio Sanatorium
creator: aalto
note: A modernist tuberculosis hospital designed around the comfort and recovery of patients.
description: Alvar Aalto won a competition in 1929 for a tuberculosis sanatorium in a pine forest near Turku, at a time when fresh air, light and rest were the main treatment. The patients' wing is a long, narrow block oriented to catch the morning sun, ending in stacked open sun balconies where patients lay for hours. Aalto designed the details from the patient's position: soft-coloured ceilings for people lying in bed, indirect lighting, quiet washbasins that splash less, and the bentwood Paimio chair, angled to ease breathing. Other wings for treatment, staff and services fan out on different angles. Antibiotics later made such sanatoria obsolete, and it became a general hospital, then closed in the 2010s. It is now used for other purposes and is on Finland's tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage status.

title: Villa Mairea
creator: aalto
note: A country house in a forest, mingling modernism with Finnish wood, stone and craft.
description: Harry and Maire Gullichsen, an industrialist couple and patrons of modern art, commissioned the Aaltos to design a house on the family estate near Pori, asking for an experiment in modern living. The L-shaped house encloses a garden with a kidney-shaped pool and a turf-roofed sauna. Inside, the large living space flows freely, its black-painted steel columns wrapped in rattan or grouped with wooden poles evoking the surrounding forest, while a stair is screened by vertical poles. White render, timber cladding, stone and a curved wooden studio mix the international and the vernacular. Villa Mairea is often described as Aalto's most personal work and an example of a softer, more humane modernism. It remains in the family and can be visited by appointment.

title: Glass House
creator: johnson
note: Philip Johnson's own house, a glass box in a landscaped estate, inspired by Mies's Farnsworth House.
description: Philip Johnson built his own home on a wooded estate in New Canaan, completing it before Mies's Farnsworth House, which he had seen in design. It is a single room, about 17 by 10 metres, with walls of glass on a steel frame painted charcoal, and a brick cylinder containing the bathroom and fireplace as its only enclosed element. Low cabinets divide living, dining and sleeping areas. Opposite stands a windowless brick guest house. Over the next fifty years Johnson added an underground painting gallery, a sculpture gallery, a pavilion on the pond, a studio and other follies across the estate, a catalogue of his changing tastes. He and his partner David Whitney lived there until their deaths in 2005, leaving it to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which opened it to the public.

title: Unité d'Habitation, Marseille
creator: le-corbusier
note: A raw-concrete 'vertical village' of 337 flats on pilotis, the founding work of Brutalism.
description: After the Second World War the French reconstruction ministry commissioned Le Corbusier to build a prototype of mass housing in Marseille. The Unité d'Habitation, also called the Cité Radieuse, is a slab of eighteen storeys on massive tapering pilotis, containing 337 apartments of twenty-three types for up to about 1,600 people. Most flats are two-storey units interlocking around internal 'streets' every third floor, with a double-height living room and a balcony on each side, shaded by deep sun-breakers. Halfway up, a street of shops and a hotel, and on the roof a nursery school, a running track, a paddling pool and sculptural ventilation stacks, make it a vertical village. Its rough board-marked concrete, béton brut, gave Brutalism its name, and its proportions follow Le Corbusier's Modulor. Variants were built in Nantes, Berlin, Briey and Firminy.

title: Notre-Dame du Haut, Ronchamp
creator: le-corbusier
note: A sculptural hilltop chapel with a billowing concrete roof and walls pierced by coloured windows.
description: A pilgrimage chapel on the hill of Bourlémont, near Belfort, was destroyed in the fighting of 1944, and the diocese, encouraged by reformers of religious art, commissioned Le Corbusier to rebuild it. Surprising those who knew his machine-age villas, he created a sculptural building of thick, curved white walls, reusing the rubble of the old chapel, under a dark concrete roof shaped like a hull or a crab shell, raised slightly on hidden posts so a thin band of light separates it from the walls. The south wall is pierced by deep, irregular windows with coloured glass. Three towers bring light down onto side altars, and an outdoor altar and pulpit serve large open-air congregations. Ronchamp's free forms divided modernists and opened the way for expressive architecture. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing of Le Corbusier's works.

title: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum
creator: wright
location: Fifth Avenue, New York City, United States
note: A spiral ramp gallery around a skylit atrium, Wright's last great work.
description: Solomon R. Guggenheim and the artist Hilla Rebay, director of his foundation for non-objective art, commissioned Wright in 1943 to design a museum. After years of revisions, delays and conflicts with building officials, it opened in October 1959, six months after Wright's death. The building is a concrete spiral, wider at the top than the bottom, facing Central Park. Inside, a continuous ramp winds up around a central atrium under a glass dome, so visitors see the art as they descend and look across the open space at other works. Many artists and critics objected that its sloping floors and curved walls made paintings hard to hang. A tower by Gwathmey Siegel was added in 1992. The museum is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Wright's architecture.

title: Seagram Building
creator: mies
location: Park Avenue, New York City, United States
note: A bronze and glass tower set back behind a plaza, the model of the modern corporate skyscraper.
description: Samuel Bronfman, head of the distillers Seagram, planned a headquarters on Park Avenue; his daughter Phyllis Lambert persuaded him to hire Mies van der Rohe, with Philip Johnson as collaborator. Mies set the 38-storey tower back from the street behind an open granite plaza with two pools, an unusual gift of space in Manhattan that influenced New York's later zoning rules. The structure is concrete-encased steel, but its façade is clad in bronze mullions and amber-tinted glass, with non-structural bronze I-beams applied to express the frame, an expensive refinement. Johnson designed the interiors, including the Four Seasons restaurant. Lavishly built and precisely detailed, the Seagram was the model for countless glass office towers worldwide.

title: Cathedral of Brasília
creator: niemeyer
note: A crown of sixteen curved concrete columns enclosing a luminous, partly sunken interior.
description: The Metropolitan Cathedral was one of the first buildings of Brazil's new capital, laid out by Lúcio Costa, and Niemeyer designed it as a hyperboloid of sixteen curving concrete columns, each weighing many tonnes, which meet at a ring and open upward like hands raised to heaven or a crown of thorns. The spaces between them are glazed, and since 1987–90 the glass has been decorated with blue, green and white stained glass by Marianne Peretti. Visitors enter through a dark passage that descends below ground and emerge into the bright circular nave, a contrast intended to lift the spirit. Four bronze evangelists by Alfredo Ceschiatti stand outside, and angels hang from steel cables inside. Its structure was completed in 1960 and it was dedicated in 1970. Brasília is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: National Congress of Brazil
creator: niemeyer
note: Twin office towers between a dome and an inverted dome, the symbol of Brazil's modern capital.
description: At the end of the Monumental Axis of Brasília, in the Square of the Three Powers, Niemeyer designed the National Congress as a horizontal platform carrying two contrasting bowls: an upturned dome over the Senate and an open, upturned saucer over the larger Chamber of Deputies, expressing the more reflective and the more open houses of parliament. Between them rise twin 28-storey office towers joined by a bridge, forming an H that has been read as standing for humanity. The building was inaugurated with the city on 21 April 1960. Its clean geometry against the sky became the symbol of Brazilian modernism and of Kubitschek's developmental optimism, and its ramps and roof have been the scene of political demonstrations, including the storming of 8 January 2023.

title: TWA Flight Center
creator: eero-saarinen
location: John F. Kennedy International Airport, New York City, United States
note: A terminal of swooping concrete shells evoking flight, now a hotel.
description: Trans World Airlines commissioned Eero Saarinen to design its terminal at what was then Idlewild Airport, and he sought to capture the excitement of flight. Four thin concrete shells, curved like wings and meeting at a central skylight, are supported on Y-shaped piers; under them, the interior flows without straight lines, with curving stairs, balconies, a sunken lounge with views of the runways, and tubular corridors to the gates, all in white tiles and red carpet. Saarinen died before it opened in 1962, and his office completed it. The terminal could not adapt to jumbo jets and security screening, and closed in 2001. Designated a New York City landmark in 1994, it reopened in 2019 as the lobby of the TWA Hotel.

title: Gateway Arch
creator: eero-saarinen
note: A stainless-steel arch 192 metres high, the tallest monument in the Western Hemisphere.
description: In 1947–48 Eero Saarinen won a competition for the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial in St Louis, commemorating the westward expansion of the United States from the city once called the Gateway to the West. His design, a weighted catenary arch, is as wide at its base as it is tall, 192 metres, and is built of triangular sections with stainless-steel outer skins and carbon-steel inner skins, filled with concrete at the lower levels. Construction began in 1963 and the last section was set in 1965, after Saarinen's death. Small capsule trams inside each leg carry visitors to an observation room at the top. The area around it became the Gateway Arch National Park in 2018.

title: Sydney Opera House
creator: utzon
note: A cluster of white sail-like shells on a harbour point, a masterpiece of twentieth-century architecture.
description: Utzon won the international competition of 1957 with sketches for a performing arts centre on a granite platform jutting into Sydney Harbour, crowned by soaring shells. The jury, including Eero Saarinen, recognised its originality, but nobody knew how to build the shells. After years of work with the engineers Ove Arup and Partners, Utzon found in 1961 a solution by deriving all their curves from the surface of a single sphere, so that they could be assembled from prefabricated ribs, and they were covered with over a million glazed white and cream tiles from Sweden. A change of state government, rising costs and disputes led to Utzon's resignation in 1966, and the interiors were completed by Peter Hall and others. Queen Elizabeth II opened it in 1973. In 2007 it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site; Utzon's son Jan has since worked on revisions toward his father's intentions.

title: Salk Institute for Biological Studies
creator: kahn
note: Twin laboratory blocks flanking a travertine plaza open to the Pacific.
description: Jonas Salk, developer of the polio vaccine, founded an institute for biological research on clifftops above the Pacific and asked Kahn for a place where scientists and artists might meet. Kahn designed two mirror-image laboratory buildings with column-free floors alternating with service floors for pipes and ducts, which can be changed as research changes. Facing an empty travertine courtyard are angled concrete towers with teak-panelled studies for the scientists. On the advice of the Mexican architect Luis Barragán, Kahn left the courtyard without trees, a 'façade to the sky', with a thin channel of water running toward the ocean. Built in finely finished concrete, the institute is among the most admired buildings of its era, and a meeting hall Kahn planned was never built.

title: National Parliament House, Dhaka (Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban)
creator: kahn
note: A monumental parliament of concrete and marble set in a lake, completed after Kahn's death.
description: In 1962 the government of Pakistan commissioned Kahn to design a second capital complex at Dhaka, then the capital of East Pakistan. After the war of independence of 1971 the new nation of Bangladesh continued the project as its parliament. The assembly building is a cluster of massive concrete volumes inlaid with bands of white marble, around the central chamber, and pierced by huge circles, triangles and rectangles that bring light into the interior and shade it from the tropical sun. A lake surrounds much of it. Kahn died in 1974, and the building was completed in 1982 by his former associates. Its story is told in his son Nathaniel Kahn's documentary My Architect (2003).

title: Louvre Pyramid
creator: pei
note: A glass and steel pyramid that became the new entrance of the Louvre.
description: President François Mitterrand's Grand Louvre project moved the finance ministry out of the palace and reorganised the museum, and he chose I. M. Pei in 1983 without a competition. Pei proposed a vast underground reception hall under the Cour Napoléon, lit and marked by a glass pyramid about 21 metres high, flanked by smaller pyramids and fountains. Its steel framework and specially made clear glass were designed for maximum transparency, so that the historic façades are seen through it. The project was fiercely attacked in France as an alien intrusion, but the pyramid, opened in 1989, became one of the most recognisable images of Paris. An inverted pyramid was added in the underground shopping arcade in 1993.

title: Bank of China Tower
creator: pei
note: A faceted skyscraper of triangular trusses, inspired by growing bamboo.
description: The Bank of China commissioned Pei, whose father had been a senior figure in the bank, to design its Hong Kong headquarters, to be finished before the handover of the colony to China in 1997. The 367-metre tower, the tallest in Asia when completed in 1990, rises from a square divided diagonally into four triangles, which terminate at different heights like the shoots of bamboo, an image of growth. Its structure is a space frame of diagonal braces expressed on the façade in triangles, which carries wind loads efficiently with much less steel than a conventional tower. Its sharp angles drew criticism from practitioners of feng shui.

title: Royal National Theatre
creator: lasdun
note: Lasdun's terraced concrete theatre on the South Bank, an icon of British Brutalism.
description: The idea of a National Theatre had been discussed for a century before Lasdun was appointed in 1963, working with a committee including Laurence Olivier and Peter Brook. The building beside Waterloo Bridge contains three theatres: the large open-stage Olivier, inspired by the theatre of Epidaurus, the proscenium Lyttelton and the flexible Cottesloe, now the Dorfman. Outside, horizontal concrete terraces project at many levels like geological strata, extending the foyers into public balconies overlooking the Thames, while fly towers rise above. The concrete is board-marked, recording the grain of the timber formwork. Opened in stages in 1976–77, the building was at first much criticised; it was listed Grade II* in 1994 and has since been renovated.

title: Barbican Estate
creator: chamberlin-powell-bon
note: A Brutalist city within the City of London, with towers, terraces, lakes and an arts centre.
description: The Cripplegate area of the City of London was destroyed by bombing in 1940, and the City Corporation decided to rebuild it as a residential district for about 4,000 people. Chamberlin, Powell and Bon designed some 2,000 flats in three triangular towers, among the tallest residential buildings in London when completed, and long terrace blocks raised on columns around lakes, gardens and the surviving medieval church of St Giles Cripplegate, with the City of London School for Girls and the Guildhall School of Music and Drama. Pedestrian walkways separate people from traffic. The arts centre, opened by the Queen in 1982, contains concert hall, theatres, cinemas, a library and a conservatory. Its bush-hammered concrete was much disliked, but the estate was listed Grade II in 2001 and is now among the most sought-after addresses in London.

title: Vanna Venturi House
creator: venturi
location: Chestnut Hill, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States
note: A house for the architect's mother, with a split gable front, one of the first postmodern buildings.
description: Robert Venturi designed this house for his widowed mother, Vanna, revising it repeatedly. Its front façade is a broad gable, split in the middle above the entrance, with a thin applied arch and a strip moulding, and windows of different shapes placed according to the rooms behind, not the symmetry of the front. Inside, a fireplace and chimney compete with the staircase for the centre of the house, and the stair narrows awkwardly around it. Small in size, the house plays with the conventional image of home, full of the complexity and contradiction Venturi was championing in his book of 1966. It received the American Institute of Architects' Twenty-five Year Award in 1989 and is often called the first postmodern building.

title: Portland Building
creator: graves
note: A cubic municipal building with giant pilasters, a keystone and pastel colours, the emblem of postmodernism.
description: The city of Portland held a design competition for a fifteen-storey municipal office building on a modest budget, judged with Philip Johnson as adviser, and Michael Graves won. On a square block he painted and applied a giant classical vocabulary: huge tapering pilasters on the façades, a stylised keystone, garlands, and colours of terracotta, blue and cream, with small square windows. Above the entrance stands Portlandia, a large copper statue by Raymond Kaskey. The building was celebrated as a turning point away from modernism and criticised for its cramped, dark interiors and leaking walls. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2011 and was extensively rebuilt between 2017 and 2020, preserving its appearance.

title: Centre Pompidou
creator: rogers
note: An inside-out cultural centre with its structure, escalators and colour-coded services on the outside.
description: President Georges Pompidou wanted a centre for modern art, books, music and design in the Beaubourg district of Paris, and Renzo Piano, Richard Rogers and Gianfranco Franchini won the international competition of 1971, with engineers from Ove Arup and Partners. They designed a flexible container of six column-free floors, 166 metres long, whose steel structure, cast steel brackets called gerberettes, bracing and services are placed outside: blue for air, green for water, yellow for electricity, red for circulation, with a glass-tube escalator climbing the façade over a sloping public square. Opened in 1977, it was likened to an oil refinery, but became one of the most visited cultural buildings in France and the founding work of high-tech architecture. It closed in 2025 for a renovation planned to last about five years.

title: Lloyd's Building
creator: rogers
note: A stainless-steel tower with lifts, stairs and ducts on the outside around a tall atrium.
description: The insurance market Lloyd's of London needed a building that could expand and adapt, and Richard Rogers designed one around a central atrium about 60 metres high under a barrel-vaulted glass roof, with the underwriting floors arranged as galleries connected by escalators. Lifts, staircases, toilets and service ducts are placed in six stainless-steel towers outside the main block, so that they can be replaced without disturbing the core, and the clear glass lift cars run on the exterior. The Adam Room, an eighteenth-century dining room, was reassembled inside. Completed in 1986, it became in 2011 the youngest building in England listed Grade I.

title: The Shard
creator: piano
note: A tapering glass tower beside London Bridge station, once the tallest building in the European Union.
description: The developer Irvine Sellar commissioned Renzo Piano to design a tower beside London Bridge station, and Piano is said to have sketched it on a napkin. The building tapers to 310 metres, its faceted glass planes splitting apart at the top, where they appear unfinished, so that the tower seems to dissolve into the sky. It contains offices, restaurants, a hotel, apartments and a public viewing gallery near the summit. Its slim, pointed form was intended to sit lightly among London's church spires, though conservation bodies objected to its effect on views of St Paul's and the Tower. On completion in 2012 it was the tallest building in the European Union.

title: HSBC Main Building, Hong Kong
creator: foster
note: A suspended steel structure with an open public plaza beneath and a sunlit atrium above.
description: The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation commissioned Norman Foster to rebuild its headquarters on Statue Square, and it was among the most expensive buildings in the world when completed. Instead of a central core, the floors hang from five sets of steel suspension trusses carried by eight masts, so that the ground floor is an open public plaza through which pedestrians pass. Escalators rise from the plaza into a tall atrium, lit by a 'sunscoop' of mirrors that reflects daylight down into it. Prefabricated parts were made around the world, and the services are in modules placed along the sides. Feng shui advisers were consulted on the design.

title: Reichstag Dome
creator: foster
note: A glass dome with a spiral ramp over the restored Reichstag, home of the German Bundestag.
description: After German reunification, the Bundestag decided to move back to the Reichstag building, completed in 1894 to a design by Paul Wallot, burned in 1933 and badly damaged in 1945. Foster and Partners won the competition to rebuild it, and the scheme was preceded by Christo and Jeanne-Claude's wrapping of the building in 1995. Inside the gutted shell, Foster created a new plenary chamber and offices, and crowned it with a glass dome, with two spiral ramps on which visitors can walk above the legislators, a symbol of transparency and democratic accountability. A mirrored cone at the centre reflects daylight into the chamber and draws out exhaust air. Graffiti by Soviet soldiers from 1945 were preserved in the interiors. It opened in 1999.

title: 30 St Mary Axe (The Gherkin)
creator: foster
note: A bullet-shaped tower with a spiralling diagonal grid of glass and steel.
description: The tower stands on the site of the Baltic Exchange, damaged by an IRA bomb in 1992. Commissioned by the reinsurance company Swiss Re, Foster and Partners designed a 41-storey tower, 180 metres high, whose circular plan swells in the middle and narrows to the top. Its diagonally braced steel structure, the diagrid, sits on the perimeter, freeing the floors of columns, and spiral light wells formed by rotating each floor plan draw air and daylight through the building, reducing energy use. Only one piece of curved glass, the lens at the summit, is used; the rest of the curve is made of flat panes. It won the RIBA Stirling Prize in 2004 and became a symbol of the City of London.

title: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
creator: gehry
note: A titanium-clad museum of sweeping curves on the river Nervión, which transformed its city.
description: The Basque government and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation agreed in 1991 to build a museum of modern and contemporary art as part of the regeneration of Bilbao, a declining industrial port. Frank Gehry's design, on a former dockland site by the river and under a road bridge, is a cluster of curved volumes clad in some 33,000 thin titanium panels, with walls of limestone and glass, around a tall atrium. Its complex forms were designed and fabricated using CATIA, software developed for aircraft design. The galleries range from classical rooms to a huge boat-shaped hall for large-scale works such as Richard Serra's The Matter of Time. After it opened in 1997 visitors flooded into Bilbao, and the term 'Bilbao effect' came to describe the hope that a spectacular building can regenerate a city.

title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
creator: gehry
note: The home of the Los Angeles Philharmonic, with billowing stainless-steel sails and a wooden auditorium.
description: Lillian Disney, widow of Walt Disney, gave an initial gift of 50 million dollars in 1987 for a concert hall in downtown Los Angeles, and Gehry won the competition in 1988. The project stalled for years over funding, and the design of the exterior changed from stone to stainless steel after Bilbao. Its curving, sail-like panels enclose foyers and gardens around a vineyard-style auditorium in which the audience surrounds the orchestra, lined with Douglas fir and designed with the acoustician Yasuhisa Toyota, with an organ of curved pipes. It opened in 2003 as the home of the Los Angeles Philharmonic. Glare from polished panels heated neighbouring buildings and they were dulled. It became a symbol of downtown Los Angeles.

title: Vitra Fire Station
creator: hadid
location: Vitra Campus, Weil am Rhein, Germany
note: Zaha Hadid's first major building, a composition of sharp, tilting concrete planes.
description: After a fire in 1981 destroyed much of the Vitra furniture company's factory at Weil am Rhein, near Basel, its chairman Rolf Fehlbaum began commissioning buildings from leading architects for the site. Zaha Hadid, then known mainly for her paintings and unbuilt projects, was asked to design a small fire station for the company's own fire brigade. She created a long, narrow building of exposed concrete planes that slant, tilt and slice past each other, like a frozen explosion of movement, with a roof canopy projecting sharply over the entrance. When local fire brigades took over, the building became a space for displaying Vitra's chair collection and events. It established Hadid's reputation as a builder.

title: Heydar Aliyev Center
creator: hadid
note: A cultural centre of continuous white curving surfaces, with no straight lines.
description: Named after the former president of Azerbaijan and father of his successor, the centre was commissioned by the government as a symbol of the modernising, oil-rich state. Zaha Hadid Architects designed a building in which the landscaped plaza seems to rise, fold and curve into a continuous white surface that becomes walls and roof, without a visible break, over a conference hall, a museum and galleries. A space frame of steel supports the cladding of glass-fibre reinforced panels, whose forms were developed digitally. The building won the Design Museum's Design of the Year award in 2014. It also drew criticism over the commissioning government's record on human rights and the evictions associated with the site.

title: Jewish Museum Berlin
creator: libeskind
note: A zigzag zinc-clad building with voids, axes and a tower of silence, a monument of memory.
description: Daniel Libeskind won the competition in 1989 for an extension to the Berlin Museum dedicated to Jewish history. The building is a zigzag in plan, like a broken Star of David, clad in zinc and cut by slashing windows. It has no entrance of its own: visitors descend from the Baroque old building into underground axes representing continuity, exile and the Holocaust, the last ending in a tall, cold, unheated tower lit only by a slit. A line of empty concrete voids cuts through the whole building and can be seen but not entered. In the Garden of Exile, visitors walk on a tilted floor among forty-nine concrete pillars with trees growing from their tops. Before any exhibits were installed, the empty building opened to visitors in 1999, and many thought it should remain empty; the museum opened in 2001.

title: Seattle Central Library
creator: koolhaas
note: A library of stacked, shifted platforms wrapped in a diamond-grid glass skin.
description: OMA, led by Rem Koolhaas with Joshua Prince-Ramus, designed Seattle's new central library by analysing the library's functions and grouping them into five stable 'platforms' stacked and shifted to fit the site, with more fluid public spaces in between. A diamond-patterned steel and glass skin stretches over the whole, creating a striking faceted form. The 'Books Spiral', a continuous ramp of shelving running through four floors, keeps the non-fiction collection in unbroken Dewey order, and a great top-lit reading room crowns the building. A bright red floor of meeting rooms and a 'living room' open to the city are among its features. It opened in 2004 and has been heavily used.

title: CCTV Headquarters
creator: koolhaas
note: A looping tower in which two leaning towers meet in a cantilevered bridge.
description: China Central Television commissioned OMA, led by Rem Koolhaas and Ole Scheeren, with the engineers Arup, for its headquarters in Beijing's new business district. Instead of a conventional skyscraper, two leaning towers rise from a common base and join at the top in a cantilevered L-shaped bridge, forming a continuous loop of spaces for the broadcaster's production, offices and services. The irregular diagonal grid on its glass skin expresses the forces in the structure, denser where stresses are greater. Its shape earned it popular nicknames, and a fire in an adjacent building in 2009 delayed its completion. The building was seen as a symbol of China's ambitions before the 2008 Olympics, and its commission for a state broadcaster provoked debate in the West.

title: City of Arts and Sciences
creator: calatrava
note: A complex of white skeletal buildings in the former bed of the river Turia.
description: After a catastrophic flood in 1957, Valencia diverted the river Turia, and its old bed became a long park. At its south-eastern end the regional government built the City of Arts and Sciences, mostly designed by Santiago Calatrava, a native of the city. Its buildings include the Hemisfèric (1998), a planetarium and IMAX cinema like a great eye with a moving lid, the Science Museum, with its rib-like structure, the Umbracle, a landscaped walkway, the Ágora, and the Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía (2005), an opera house under a huge feather-like crest, set among shallow pools. The oceanographic park was designed by Félix Candela. The complex became a symbol of Valencia and a tourist attraction, but its cost overruns and maintenance problems, such as the loss of mosaic tiles from the opera house, have been widely criticised.

title: Tate Modern
creator: herzog-de-meuron
type: Art museum in a former power station
note: A power station converted into a museum of modern art, with a vast Turbine Hall.
description: Bankside Power Station, designed by Giles Gilbert Scott and built in stages from 1947 to 1963, closed in 1981. The Tate chose it for a new museum of modern and contemporary art, and Herzog & de Meuron won the competition in 1995 with a scheme that preserved the brick building and its tall chimney. They turned the former Turbine Hall into a vast covered street and space for commissioned installations, and added a two-storey light beam of glass along the roof. Tate Modern opened in 2000, received many more visitors than expected, and helped transform the South Bank. The architects added the Blavatnik Building, a twisted pyramid of perforated brick, in 2016. It is among the most visited museums of modern art in the world.

title: Elbphilharmonie
creator: herzog-de-meuron
note: A wave-crested glass concert hall built on top of a brick harbour warehouse.
description: The Elbphilharmonie stands on the tip of a peninsula in Hamburg's harbour, on top of the Kaispeicher A, a brick warehouse of the 1960s for cocoa, tea and tobacco. Herzog & de Meuron raised a glass structure on it whose roof rises and falls like waves, made of curved panes partly printed with dots. Between the old warehouse and the new building, a public plaza 37 metres above the ground gives views over the city and harbour. Inside are a hotel, apartments and three concert halls; the great hall, with seats rising in vineyard terraces around the stage, is lined with 10,000 gypsum panels individually milled to scatter sound, designed with the acoustician Yasuhisa Toyota. Costs rose from an estimated 77 million to about 789 million euros and the opening was delayed by years, but since 2017 it has become a symbol of Hamburg.
